Many publishers are responding to a new reality on the open web: Bot traffic is rivaling traffic from human readers.

According to recent reports, one of the world’s largest business publishers is shutting the door on unwelcome bots. In May, Dow Jones overhauled its bot strategy and now disallows all bots by default, the company told Nieman Lab. The latest bot permissions apply to all of its free and paid consumer news sites, including The Wall Street Journal, Barron’s, and MarketWatch.

It has been revealed that as part of the shift, the company revised each site’s robots.txt file — a webpage that tells bots which parts of a site they can and can’t access. Rather than reactively blacklisting bots through robots.txt, Dow Jones now operates with a whitelist for select crawlers and scrapers.

“As bot traffic has shifted from discovery-oriented use cases toward systems that can ingest, summarize, or otherwise benefit from our content without a relationship in place, we have moved to a more deliberate signal,” noted Nolly Evans, chief development officer at Dow Jones. “[This] signals to third parties that they must negotiate and partner directly with us for content access.”.

The Wall Street Journal’s whitelist contains more than 60 bots, including search engine crawlers and three scrapers operated by OpenAI, which has a $250 million-plus licensing deal with Dow Jones’ parent manufacturer, News Corp.

“We’re seeing astronomical growth in bot traffic while human referrals and traffic to news sites are being curtailed,” mentioned Evans. “That’s a clear signal to publishers that the old norms are no longer working, and that something needs to change.”.

Robots.txt files are voluntary guidance for all bots, including those deployed by AI companies. They’re not hard technical blocks or legally binding contracts. Some AI companies, like Perplexity, have used “stealth crawlers” to bypass robots.txt files while evading detection. Still, The Journal isn’t alone in using robots.txt to disallow bots by default, whether to create friction for scrapers, as leverage to negotiate for content licensing deals, or to minimize the burden on their servers.

An analysis of the robots.txt files of 1,000 leading English-language publishers websites by the bot analytics company Known Agents demonstrates that about 2% of those sites now disallow all bots by default, including Reuters, Bloomberg Law, Publishers Weekly, and the British technology news site The Register.

Industry observers note that many of these publications are owned by News Corp, including several of the organization’s Australian newspapers (The Australian, The Daily Telegraph in Sydney, the Herald Sun in Melbourne) and its marquee U.K. papers (The Times, The Sun, The Scottish Sun).

“One of the most key challenges for us is making sure that the IP journalists create is respected by the AI companies,” News Corp CEO Robert Thomson said in an interview with CNBC last week. “The principled companies want to have an agreement, and the unprincipled companies don’t. We’ll try to convince you to be transactional and pay us for our IP and pay us for our journalism, or we’ll sue you.”.

More and more publishers are opting to restrict bots using whitelists. Late last year, The Atlantic told Digiday that it only allows bots associated with its licensing deals or those that drive significant traffic to the website. In June, Digiday first reported that Reuters and Time had started issuing whitelists of their own.

People Inc. has been vocal about its decision to go beyond robots.txt files and hard-block bots by default. When the company made the switch at the beginning of this year, it went from blocking 2,000 unique bots to more than 30,000.

Sources indicate that many of these publishers are responding to a new reality on the open web: Bot traffic is rivaling traffic from human readers. Over the past 90 days, around 34% of pageviews across more than 5,000 randomly selected websites came from bots, according to an index maintained by Known Agents. About 29% of those bots were “AI-related” (e.g. AI agents, AI chatbots, and AI training scrapers), as opposed to more traditional bots like search engine crawlers and archivers operated by the Wayback Machine.

Despite some publishers wanting to restrict AI-related bot traffic, many aren’t making full use of their robots.txt files to do so, according to Gavin King, the CEO of Known Agents. The company started as a free crowdsourced database to help identify bots, but now offers publishers analytic tools and other products to monitor and control bot traffic.

Known Agents at the moment tracks more than 2,000 AI-related bots, but the majority of English-language news publishers only restrict a fraction of those on their robots.txt files.

“Robots.txt is the easiest first line of defense,” noted King. “The fact that people are reaching out to [internet infrastructure companies to sign] six-figure year contracts instead of updating their robots.txt for free is such a miss.”.

King acknowledged that robots.txt alone can’t stop content from being scraped without permission or compensation. But he also pointed to clients who have reduced traffic from known AI-related bots by more than 90% by updating their robots.txt file with a more comprehensive list.

In a recent development, “It’s been such a manual process,” remarked King. “Everyone is doing it individually, in-house instead of automating the process.”.

Slate is one of the publications that has leaned on Known Agents’ “Automated Robots.txt” to try to stem the tide of AI bots to its site. Slate’s small product team uses the free version of the tool to access Known Agents’ API weekly and review any newly discovered bots or renamed agents that have been added to the company’s database. The tool automatically revises its robots.txt file based on that review.

According to recent reports, “We have almost 30 years of content, which is a long history of being online,” Greg Lavallee, Slate’s VP of technology, remarked. “We’re seeing no value from bots and it costs us bandwidth fees, so we decided to tell them not to bother.”.

It has been revealed that lavallee noted that since September, preliminary data shows that several bots have ignored the publication’s robots.txt and continue to attempt to crawl its website, though he declined to name the exact bots. Slate is exploring “server-side paywall strategies that will make it more difficult for scrapers to access full content,” he said.

Slate at the moment has no licensing deals with major AI companies, despite active outreach to buyers in the past.

“It’s very easy for us to take that robots.txt list and go look at the [server] logs and say, ‘We told you not to access and then you did,” noted Lavallee. “I feel like you have to [update your Robots.txt file], but it’s definitely not enough. Something more needs to happen than asking nicely.”.

💡 Key Takeaways

  • In 9 AI Workflows That Turn Marketing Data Into Content AI Cites, Ryann Hogan, director of growth marketing at CallRail, and Jay Schwedelson, founder and CEO of Guru Media Hub, tackled two sides of the same problem: how to find something worth publishing and how to tell whether the right people found it.
  • Industry observers note that hogan used customer conversations to explain what a traffic report can miss.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, if customers keep asking whether you offer a service, you have a brief for a landing page. You also have the words people use to describe what they need. That gives an editor a better starting point than asking AI to come up with a topic from scratch.

In 9 AI Workflows That Turn Marketing Data Into Content AI Cites, Ryann Hogan, director of growth marketing at CallRail, and Jay Schwedelson, founder and CEO of Guru Media Hub, tackled two sides of the same problem: how to find something worth publishing and how to tell whether the right people found it.

Industry observers note that hogan used customer conversations to explain what a traffic report can miss. A campaign might generate plenty of calls, but how many ended in a booked appointment? A caller might also say a neighbor recommended the business. The campaign that brought someone to the phone and the reason they knew to look for the company are both useful, but they answer different questions.

See the full on-demand clip at 15:55.

Sources indicate that hogan suggested looking for recurring service questions in call summaries. If people keep asking whether a business does a particular kind of work, a page that answers that question in their own terms gives them a reason to visit. If a keyword generates inquiries from people who need something else entirely, the better decision may be to move the budget rather than write more copy.

She applied the same principle to outreach. Before writing a personalized opener, her team checked whether the prospect was in a market it served and offered the services its software supported. She recommended trying the criteria on ten accounts and inspecting the results before running them across a list.

According to recent reports, hogan distinguished between a saved set of instructions and a connector. The first tells the AI how the team writes: examples of its voice, phrases to avoid, the structure of a page and the fields an editor expects. The second lets it do something with that work, such as placing the copy in the right fields in WordPress.

An attendee asked whether that meant giving AI permission to publish. Hogan mentioned her team used draft access and recommended checking with IT and security before connecting a CMS. The editor checked that the copy landed in the right fields, but the review went beyond proofreading. A relevant video, for example, could answer a reader’s question better than another paragraph.

It has been revealed that schwedelson stated lists, how-to guides and original research stood out in his team’s review of content cited by AI tools. For a page already on the site, he demonstrated how he asked an AI tool to identify the passages it could use to answer a question and the ones that added little. The result was an editing suggestion, not proof that the page had been cited.

See the full on-demand clip at 24:35.

He also suggested testing a change on some pages before rolling it out everywhere. For a set of evergreen articles, he proposed adding a date to the headlines of genuinely updated pieces, leaving a comparison group alone, then comparing traffic over 30 days. In the Q&A he clarified that the date should reflect the current period, not a future one. A difference in traffic would give an editor something to investigate. It would not establish that a date earned an AI citation.

When an attendee asked what a good citation rate looked like, Hogan declined to name a universal target. She suggested comparing performance with the previous month. Schwedelson added a useful check: look at why a business was cited. More mentions for a service it does not offer are hardly a win. Hogan’s preferred measure, where attribution was possible, was whether the marketing produced revenue.

In a recent development, hogan described a recurring report that refreshed the figures in Google Sheets before she opened it. She used that data to patch monthly slides, but kept the judgment about what had changed and what to tell her boss. Hogan explained the distinction: “We still own the numbers. AI is doing the pulling, the formatting, the hard stuff, and then we’re doing the analysis.” See the full on-demand clip at 20:08.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • When HubSpot’s blog lost about 80% of its organic traffic to AI, revenue still grew nearly 20%.
  • It has been revealed that in his interview with Greg Jarboe for Search Engine Journal, CMO Kipp Bodnar explained why.
  • As a result, those newer channels now bring in about 90% of HubSpot’s content leads, with the blog accounting for roughly 10%.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

When HubSpot’s blog lost about 80% of its organic traffic to AI, revenue still grew nearly 20%.

It has been revealed that in his interview with Greg Jarboe for Search Engine Journal, CMO Kipp Bodnar explained why. In short, HubSpot had been building an audience outside search since 2021: a podcast network in 2021, a newsletter acquisition the same year, a creator program in 2022, and a YouTube network in 2023.

As a result, those newer channels now bring in about 90% of HubSpot’s content leads, with the blog accounting for roughly 10%.

Recent findings suggest that I’ve spent six years inside one of those channels. The agency I founded has produced more than 300 B2B podcasts since 2019 and booked more than 2,500 guest appearances for the companies behind them. (Disclosure: All first-hand figures in this article come from that work.) Reading the interview, what struck me wasn’t the traffic drop. Instead, it was that HubSpot’s recovery ran on the channel I know best, and that most of the patterns Bodnar described show up in our data every month, including the uncomfortable ones.

Industry observers note that so this article is about what a podcast does for a B2B organization that a search result can’t. I’ve organized it around the four things a buyer has to do before they buy from you: notice you, hear you, trust you, and name you. It also covers where podcasts fail because a lot of them do!

Sources indicate that bodnar’s most useful admission was that much of HubSpot’s lost traffic “was never going to turn into revenue.” For example, posts on famous quotes and emojis drew millions of visitors who would never buy software. When AI Overviews answered those questions directly, the visits disappeared, and very few of them were potential customers.

The mechanism is now well documented. Pages ranking first lose 58% of their clicks when an AI Overview appears, according to Ahrefs, up from 34.5% in its April 2025 run. Similarly, Pew Research found consumers click a standard result 8% of the time when a summary appears, against 15% without.

However, the important point is not that clicks fell. It is that search was always a weak way to build the thing B2B buyers actually use to decide: trust in a specific tech giant, earned from people they already believe.

Reddit and SurveyMonkey’s 2026 research found 73% of B2B decision-makers trust peer recommendations, more than vendor websites at 55%. Meanwhile, Gartner found 61% of B2B buyers prefer a rep-free buying experience. In other words, buyers want to learn from people like them, without being sold to. A 40-minute conversation between two practitioners is exactly that, in a form Google never ranked well, and AI engines are citing more and more.

See also: The Dangerous Seduction Of Click-Chasing.

First, a podcast has to get a buyer to notice the firm behind it. This is where most B2B shows fail, and I’ve watched this many times.

A organization rolls out a show. The CEO hosts. Twelve episodes later, downloads are flat at 150 per episode, the CEO is bored, and the show quietly stops. The conclusion drawn is “podcasts don’t work for us.” In reality, the problem is that the show launched into nothing.

Sources indicate that across the highlights we’ve produced, the ones that grow are the ones that start with an audience to grow from. Specifically, two things happen before episode one. The host appears as a guest on other shows the target buyers already listen to, so the first listeners arrive from a voice they trust. And the guest list is built from people with their own audiences, who then share the episode they’re in.

HubSpot did a version of this at scale. The creator program and the podcast network were built years before the search traffic fell, so there was an audience waiting. Bodnar’s line that “no AEO trick would have covered an 80% hole” is therefore the same lesson at a different size.

See also: The New Organic Growth Stack: Search, Social, Communities & AI.

The second job is getting the buyer to listen.

According to recent reports, instantly’s 2026 benchmark puts the average cold email reply rate at 3.43% across its platform, with the top 10% of senders getting past 10%. Instantly sells outbound software, so it has no reason to make those numbers look worse than they are.

A podcast appearance inverts the dynamic. The buyer pressed play and they chose to spend 20 or 40 minutes with your leader, often while doing something else. A host they already trust vouched for your leader in the first 30 seconds.

Industry observers note that when we track what happens after client appearances, the pattern is consistent. Inquiries arrive weeks later and quote the episode. In other words, the buyer heard the whole argument before they ever spoke to sales.

For example, we regularly see leads come inbound to our clients saying: “I loved the episode on X with Y, I’d love to chat about Y for our business.”.

In a recent development, the same applies to a company’s own show once it has listeners. Edison Research’s Infinite Dial 2026 puts monthly podcast listening at 58% of Americans aged 12 and over. The audience exists, but the question is whether your show gives them a reason to be in it, which brings us to the guests.

In a recent development, the most reliable finding across our shows is also the one most companies resist. The fastest way into a buyer’s world is to interview them. Not a thought leader, not a partner, not a customer success story. The person you want to sell to.

One client, a risk-management software manufacturer, launched a weekly show in September 2025 hosted by its CEO, with guests drawn from the safety and risk leaders at its target accounts. (Disclosure: The company is a client of my agency, and these figures are from its public case study.) Twelve months later, roughly 20% of guests have become paying customers. The company also reported a 3.5x return on closed deals in the first six months, with more in the pipeline. Listeners who were never guests have become customers too, citing specific episodes as the reason they reached out.

Industry observers note that what made it work wasn’t production quality. Rather, it was three operational choices: a CEO who turned up every week, a conversation format that sets up a follow-up without being a pitch, and a post-recording workflow that got the sales team involved within days of each interview.

Recent findings suggest that remove any of the three and the show becomes content. With all three, it is a pipeline channel that happens to publish audio.

This is also the part of podcasting that search can’t replicate, and never could. A buyer who spends an hour as a guest on your show has a relationship with your company. By contrast, a buyer who clicked your blog post has a session.

See also: How To Run A Webinar Program That Actually Drives ROI.

The fourth outcome is the one Search Engine Journal readers will care about most, because it is where podcasts and AI search meet.

It has been revealed that bodnar made two points about how HubSpot gets cited in AI answers. First, the engines lean on sources that aren’t your site: Reddit, LinkedIn, YouTube, and review sites. Second, prompts now run 40 to 100 words, so content has to “answer the full question in plain, chunked language, the way a buyer would ask it.” Consequently, HubSpot moved from “The Ultimate Guide to Content Marketing” to hyper-specific pieces built around real buyer situations.

A podcast produces both of those things as a by-product. Every guest appearance is a mention, a link in show notes, and a transcript on someone else’s domain, which is the third-party presence engines weigh. Likewise, every episode of your own show is a transcript of a real buyer describing a real problem in their own words. That is the specific, first-party material engines can’t find anywhere else.

It has been revealed that we tested this on our own site. From June 1, 2026, we published one page a day written from our episode transcripts and case studies. Over the following months, our daily AI citations, which had sat between roughly 40 and 80 a day since the previous November, climbed to between 250 and 350 a day by October, and the number of our pages being cited rose from about 15 to around 60:.

Daily AI citations and cited pages for the author’s website, November 2025 to October 2026. Image created by the author.

That mentioned, I’d be cautious about the size of that effect. The base was small, and Bodnar is right that attribution here is correlative. But the direction matched what HubSpot saw: AI-answer visitors converting at roughly three times the rate of traditional search, because the buyer has already had the conversation.

The practical implication for anyone running SEO is a show’s transcripts are a content source your competitors cannot copy, and the guest appearances are citations you don’t have to pitch for. Yet most companies with podcasts are sitting on both and using neither.

The wins above come with a long tail of shows that didn’t make it. Three failures account for most of them.

The show rolls out before anyone has borrowed an audience or booked the host on other demonstrates. Twelve episodes, then silence. This is the majority of B2B podcast failures.

Industry observers note that downloads are the podcast equivalent of the sessions Bodnar says HubSpot watched for 15 years. They are inflated by bots and repeat fetches, and they say nothing about who listened.

Sources indicate that instead, the numbers that matter are which companies are listening, which guests became opportunities, and whether prospects mention the show when they inquire. If your hosting can’t tell you the first of those, you are flying blind.

The interview ends, the episode publishes, and then the guest never hears from the manufacturer again. The 20% conversion rate above came from a workflow, not a microphone.

It has been revealed that greg Jarboe ended his write-up of the interview by arguing that the goal has changed. Inbound marketing was about showing up when a buyer searched. Now the buyer asks an AI first, and your organization has to be the one they pick afterward. I agree, and I’d add that search alone can’t solve that problem.

In a recent development, buyers choose companies they have noticed, heard, trusted, and seen named. The places those four things happen are feeds, demonstrates, and AI answers, not result pages.

A podcast is the one channel that can do all four at once. It borrows an audience through guesting, earns listening time no outbound sequence can, builds relationships with the buyers you interview, and produces the specific, first-party content AI engines cite. However, it is also slow, operationally demanding, and easy to do badly, which is why most of them stop at episode 12.

HubSpot built these channels with a large marketing team and a head start of several years. Most B2B companies have neither. That is an argument for starting now, not for not starting.

So before you count downloads, count buyers. How many of the people you want to sell to have been on your show, or listened to it?

    #158546. Tech Report: Paid Search Has An AI Blind Spot – IAB Blueprint States A Claim Is Not Credit via @sejournal, @gregjarboe

    📅 27 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 9m • 📚 Deep Dive (1785 w)
    📖 Baca
    AI & Tech ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Searchenginejournal ↗ Open Full Page

    Tech Report: Paid Search Has An AI Blind Spot – IAB Blueprint States A Claim Is Not Credit via @sejournal, @gregjarboe

    📅 27 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 9 min read (1785 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Searchenginejournal

    ⏱️ ~9 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • If your branded search campaigns have posted their best return on ad spend of the year, the Interactive Advertising Bureau (IAB) has a question you should answer before you ask for more budget.
    • 12, the IAB released its AI-Era Attribution Blueprint, a framework for sorting out what role AI played when someone buys something.
    • ChatGPT answer can create the intent, a branded query can capture it, and your Google Ads account can book the conversion as a brand campaign win.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    If your branded search campaigns have posted their best return on ad spend of the year, the Interactive Advertising Bureau (IAB) has a question you should answer before you ask for more budget. Who, or what, created that demand in the first place?

    On Nov. 12, the IAB released its AI-Era Attribution Blueprint, a framework for sorting out what role AI played when someone buys something. The report cites Similarweb data showing that consumers who got a brand recommendation from an AI assistant were 2.5 times more likely to visit that brand’s website within seven days. Only 8.8% of those visits came directly from AI referrals. Search was credited with 55.9% of them, and direct traffic with 19.9%.

    ChatGPT answer can create the intent, a branded query can capture it, and your Google Ads account can book the conversion as a brand campaign win.

    In a recent development, the blueprint won’t tell you how much of your brand revenue fits that description. What it does give you is a standard of evidence for finding out, plus a few habits worth adopting in your accounts before the 2027 planning cycle locks in.

    The framework asks three questions of each conversion. Who or what created the intent? Who or what made the decision? Who or what completed the purchase?

    Industry observers note that the answers put the conversion in one of three pathways, labeled Human-Owned, AI-Assisted, and AI-Executed. According to AdExchanger’s account of the document:.

    Industry observers note that the pathway then decides which parties are eligible to make a “decision claim” or a “contributory claim,” and what evidence each claim needs. The IAB’s release says, “A claim is not credit; it is the right to be evaluated for credit.”.

    Caroline Giegerich, the IAB’s VP of AI, framed the problem in terms every search marketer will recognize.

    “AI-influenced sales are sometimes reported as search or direct traffic, which can send the next marketing investment to the wrong channel,” she said in the announcement. She added that the blueprint is meant to work alongside existing attribution systems, defining the extra credit claims AI creates and the evidence each one requires.

    It has been revealed that in other words, nobody is asking you to rip out data-driven attribution. The blueprint sits on top of it.

    The document also changed shape while it was being written. Giegerich told Digiday she went in expecting the working group to work out how credit gets assigned, and the document became “more of a call to action to the industry” instead. Digiday reported the effort took about four months and named working group members including People Inc., Walmart, WPP Media, Emberos, Criteo, Bluefish, Microsoft, Brandlight, Tinuiti, and Prudential Financial.

    Google is not among the members Digiday named, which matters for anyone hoping the largest search ad platform will start labeling AI-originated activity the way the blueprint asks.

    See also: AI Visibility Measurement: What To Track & What To Ignore.

    The IAB grounded the release in its own buyer research. In the 2026 Outlook Study: September Patch, 45% of ad buyers named comparing AI-driven and traditional customer journeys as their top measurement challenge, and 44% remarked they rely on branded search and direct traffic as proxies for AI influence they can’t track.

    Google’s own numbers show why this is getting harder to ignore. Alphabet reported Q3 2026 Google Search & other revenue of $63.35 billion, up 12% year-over-year, while CEO Sundar Pichai said Search query growth was the fastest it has been in five years. On the earnings call, chief business officer Philipp Schindler pointed to lower monetization of fast-growing AI Mode queries as one factor in the slower revenue growth, alongside currency effects, which he called the largest factor. More queries are flowing through AI surfaces, and the trail from those surfaces to the conversion is thinner than the trail from a classic results page.

    Here is my perspective. The most useful line in the blueprint for PPC managers, is that a claim is not credit. Platform attribution has blurred those two ideas for as long as I’ve covered this business, since 2003. Google Ads data-driven attribution spreads credit across the Google touchpoints it can observe. It cannot observe the ChatGPT conversation that sent someone to type your brand name. So, the report you trust most has a blind spot exactly where the new demand is being created.

    See also: When Attribution Looks More Precise Than The Data Behind It.

    Before anyone builds a budget case on 55.9%, it helps to know where that figure comes from.

    Industry observers note that it originates in Similarweb’s June 2026 study, “The Downstream Impact of AI Visibility.” It used Similarweb’s U.S. desktop panel from July through December 2025, looked at ChatGPT recommendations, and studied three verticals through brand pairs (American Express and Capital One, Skyscanner and Kayak, Sephora and Ulta). Consumers who named the brand in their own prompt were excluded.

    In a recent development, search accounted for 55.9% of AI-influenced visits versus 40.4% of visits that weren’t AI-influenced, a gap of 15.5 points. Direct traffic went the other way, 19.9% versus 38.8%. AI-influenced visitors also viewed about 12 pages per visit, compared with 6.5 for everyone else.

    There are limits a practitioner should keep in view. The panel is desktop only, while a large share of shopping happens on phones. It covers ChatGPT, not Claude, Copilot, Gemini, or Google’s own AI Mode. Six brands is a small sample, and the published figures I could find report “search” as a channel without splitting paid clicks from organic ones, so nobody should claim from this study that a specific share went to Google Ads.

    One more caution about the IAB survey. MediaPost reported that 44% of buyers named adapting to changing consumer behavior, including AI-driven search, as their top investment challenge. The release for the blueprint cites 44% relying on branded search and direct traffic as proxies. Same study, same percentage, different questions.

    Google Analytics added an “AI Assistant” channel to GA4’s Default Channel Group in May 2026, which sorts sessions from recognized chatbot referrers into their own row. It’s a real improvement, but it works on referrers. The shopper who reads a ChatGPT answer, opens a upcoming tab, and searches your brand shows up as Paid Search or Organic Search, never as AI Assistant. That is the exact behavior the Similarweb data describes.

    It has been revealed that see also: 81.8% Of My ‘AI Assistant’ Traffic Was Fake. The Googlebot Number Was Worse.

    According to recent reports, in the first edition of YouTube and Video Marketing, published in 2009, I quoted Galileo on page 337. “Count what is countable, measure what is measurable. What is not measurable, make measurable.” I’ve repeated it to students and clients ever since, because I haven’t found a better summary of what a marketer’s job is.

    The IAB blueprint reads like a working version of it for paid search.

    Count what is countable. Clicks, conversions, and sessions with an AI referrer are all countable, and your accounts already count them well.

    Measure what is measurable. Whether your brand campaigns create sales or simply catch them on the way to checkout can be measured with lift tests and holdouts. Most advertisers just haven’t done it.

    Then comes the hard part: What is not measurable, make measurable. Nobody outside the AI platforms can observe the ChatGPT conversation that sent a shopper to type your brand name into Google. The blueprint’s answer is to classify that conversion anyway, attach a claim to it, and spell out the evidence the claim would need. That is how something unmeasurable starts becoming measurable. It also tells you exactly what to ask for when the AI platforms are ready to share.

    None of this requires the AI platforms to cooperate first. Here are four steps you can take now.

    1. Estimate your pathway mix. The blueprint’s first ask of brands is to estimate the share of their conversions in each pathway. The cheapest way to start is to ask customers. Add AI assistant options (ChatGPT, Gemini, Google AI Mode, Copilot, Claude) to your post-purchase survey or lead form’s “how did you hear about us” question. Store the answer in your CRM. If you already import offline conversions, you can bring a self-reported “AI-assisted” signal into Google Ads as a separate conversion action set to secondary, so you can see it by campaign without letting it steer Smart Bidding.

    2. Put brand campaigns through an incrementality test. Google Ads help documentation now lists Search and Performance Max as supported campaign types for user-based Conversion Lift, with thresholds of at least 1,000 observed conversions and a minimum study campaign budget of $5,000. The same page still notes that Conversion Lift isn’t available for every account, so check with your rep. If you don’t qualify, a geo-based holdout on brand terms will tell you something useful. A lift test won’t classify the AI pathway for you. It will tell you how much of what your brand campaign claims would have happened anyway, which is the question you need answered before brand spend absorbs more of the budget.

    Recent findings suggest that 3. Report two columns, not one. The blueprint asks agencies to apply a single claim-and-evidence standard across platforms and to separate platform-reported claims from independently verified ones. Do that in your next Quarterly Business Review (QBR). Show Google Ads-reported brand conversions next to lift-tested incremental conversions, and show GA4’s AI Assistant sessions next to your survey’s self-reported AI share. When the columns disagree, that disagreement is the finding.

    In a recent development, 4. Ask your platform reps how AI traffic is labeled. The blueprint asks AI platforms to disclose whether recommendations are paid or organic, to name the sources behind them, and to label AI-originated traffic consistently. Put those questions to your Google and Microsoft Advertising reps directly, especially about how clicks and conversions from ads in AI Mode and Copilot surface in your reports. Microsoft sat on the working group. Its answers may come faster.

    The IAB is candid that this is a framework, not a fix. CEO David Cohen said the blueprint “is honest about what the industry can’t yet substantiate.” Much of the evidence needed to support AI claims either isn’t captured or sits inside the AI platforms.

    It has been revealed that I’d go further. The PPC managers who wait for ChatGPT, Gemini, and AI Mode to hand over clean, labeled data will spend 2027 defending brand budgets with numbers they can’t explain to a CFO. The ones who start estimating their pathway mix now, with surveys, lift tests, and two-column reporting, will at least be counting the right things.

    #158536. Industry News: Google Adds Shopping Campaigns To Promotion Mode Eligibility via @sejournal, @MattGSouthern

    📅 27 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 3m • 📚 Deep Dive (628 w)

    Industry News: Google Adds Shopping Campaigns To Promotion Mode Eligibility via @sejournal, @MattGSouthern

    📅 27 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (628 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Searchenginejournal

    ⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Retailers using standard Shopping campaigns can now schedule a lower Target ROAS and, if they choose, add extra daily budget for a 3- to 14-day sale with Promotion Mode, according to Google’s updated help page.
    • The page indicates Promotion Mode is supported for “standard Search, Shopping, and Performance Max campaigns” and is in an open beta.
    • Recent findings suggest that shopping wasn’t part of the beta at launch.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Retailers using standard Shopping campaigns can now schedule a lower Target ROAS and, if they choose, add extra daily budget for a 3- to 14-day sale with Promotion Mode, according to Google’s updated help page.

    The page indicates Promotion Mode is supported for “standard Search, Shopping, and Performance Max campaigns” and is in an open beta.

    Recent findings suggest that shopping wasn’t part of the beta at launch. Google’s June 15 announcement said, “This beta is available for Search and Performance Max campaigns.” SEJ’s Brooke Osmundson reported the beta that day.

    According to recent reports, as of Nov. 27, the page in several other languages, including German, French and Spanish, still lists only Search and Performance Max, and the English page doesn’t say when Shopping support was added.

    Recent findings suggest that the Target ROAS for a campaign will be lowered by a tolerance of 5% to 90% in Promotion Mode. In the page’s example, a Target ROAS of 500% with a 20% tolerance would equal a fresh Target ROAS of 400%.

    According to recent reports, you may add an extra amount to spend each day above your baseline on an average daily budget; however, this isn’t available on a campaign total budget. To increase spending on a campaign total budget during a promotion, you’ll need to raise the total manually.

    Google’s June launch example highlights where advertisers set promotion dates, Target ROAS tolerance, and the optional extra daily budget.

    Recent findings suggest that target ROAS bidding must be enabled at the campaign level. Portfolio bid strategies and shared budgets are not currently supported. Campaigns which have run experiments previously are also unable to use Promotion Mode.

    Sources indicate that regardless of whether Exploration has been toggled on for a campaign, Smart Bidding Exploration will automatically be on while it’s running in Promotion Mode. When Exploration is enabled before a campaign enters Promotion Mode, the two settings’ tolerances will be combined. In Google’s example, 20% plus 20% makes 40%.

    In Performance Max campaigns running Promotion Mode, Google’s help documentation explains that Smart Bidding Exploration “applies to both Search and Shopping inventory” as well as text and Shopping ads. However, if a campaign is largely serving on other networks, you may see less impact from this Smart Bidding feature. The page’s translations into various languages still say that the exploration begins with only Search inventory.

    The English version also details where an active promotion is shown (campaign settings, campaign tables, the Seasonality Adjustment menu and the bid strategy and budget reports) and indicates these changes are being rolled out incrementally and may not be available in all accounts at this time.

    Retailers that lower Shopping targets and raise daily budgets manually during a sale can schedule these changes in advance and have them revert once the sale has concluded.

    According to recent reports, as for timing, Google’s page notes upcoming campaigns should be created at least 48 hours in advance of a promotion’s start date, and existing campaigns should operate for at least one complete conversion cycle on a daily budget before turning on Promotion Mode. After an active promotion begins, its start date cannot be modified, and changes to the Target ROAS and average daily budget will need to be done through the Promotion Mode settings. Further, Google recommends avoiding CPC bid caps and suggests allowing 1-2 conversion cycles once a promotion ends for Smart Bidding to adjust to large target or budget changes.

    When measuring results from a Promotion Mode sale, Google indicates to account for the lowered target in the bid strategy report. A promotion can be ended early, and once it’s running, its end date can move as long as the whole promotion stays within 14 days.

    #158527. Google’s 404 Guide States 410s Generally Get Crawled Less Often via @sejournal, @MattGSouthern

    📅 27 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 3m • 📚 Deep Dive (519 w)
    📖 Baca
    AI & Tech ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Searchenginejournal ↗ Open Full Page

    Google’s 404 Guide States 410s Generally Get Crawled Less Often via @sejournal, @MattGSouthern

    📅 27 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (519 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Searchenginejournal

    ⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Recent findings suggest that returning a 410 status code for a removed page “generally leads to less frequent crawling,” according to Google’s updated guide to crawling errors.
    • 27 in a new section on deciding whether to fix 404 errors reported in Search Console.
    • Most of the section revisits advice Google had already shared, but its 410 line offers a different take from the Help page.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Recent findings suggest that returning a 410 status code for a removed page “generally leads to less frequent crawling,” according to Google’s updated guide to crawling errors. For indexing, Google treats 404 and 410 the same.

    The line arrived on Nov. 27 in a new section on deciding whether to fix 404 errors reported in Search Console. The documentation changelog says the section brings 404 guidance over from the Search Console Help Center into Search Central documentation, and the old Help page now redirects to the guide.

    Most of the section revisits advice Google had already shared, but its 410 line offers a different take from the Help page. The retired page read, “Presently Google treats 410s (Gone) the same as 404s (Not found).”.

    Google’s fresh guidelines have separated crawling of pages with 404 or 410 status codes from how they are indexed by Google. For a URL that was crawled by Google but returned a 404 status code, Google’s crawlers “might continue checking it occasionally,” the guide claims. The frequency of crawling is generally reduced once Google receives a 410 status code, and a 410 is treated like a 404 when it comes to indexing.

    Recent findings suggest that when I covered John Mueller’s comments on the two codes in April 2024, he called the difference in processing “so minimal” that he couldn’t think of a time he’d prefer one over the other for SEO purposes. The new guide keeps the codes equal for indexing and names a difference in crawling.

    Google’s guide puts the crawl-frequency distinction in its advice on removing URLs from sitemaps.

    The rest of the latest section repeats points from the old Help page and from a Google video embedded in the guide. One of them is a warning against blocking 404 URLs in robots.txt, since Google has to crawl a URL to see its status code. Roger Montti covered the video on Oct. 29.

    For removed pages, the crawling errors guide says to take the URLs out of sitemaps. For live pages that shouldn’t appear in Search, Google’s sitemaps overview now says leaving a URL out of a sitemap “doesn’t prevent Google from crawling or indexing it” when other pages link to it. The overview points to noindex for those pages instead.

    Sources indicate that sites bulk removing pages, such as an archive of discontinued products, can use a documented crawl difference when deciding which pages should receive a 404 vs. a 410 for content that is permanently deleted. According to Google’s crawling error guidelines, regardless of which of these codes you use, the code will not limit a site’s crawl capacity, and previously crawled 404 URLs “don’t meaningfully consume crawl budget.”.

    Whichever you decide on, delete your old URLs from your sitemaps and do not block them in robots.txt.

    Google’s guide doesn’t specify how much less often URLs that return a 410 are crawled. A site that retires many pages can explore the impact in its server logs by returning a 410 for one group of similar removed URLs and a 404 for another.

As capacity allows, you will also support the broader Commercial Legal team on other matters.

    Apply and further build out our playbook and risk framework independently, and escalate to the Assistant General Counsel, Commercial where a deal falls outside approved positions or raises novel legal risk.

    Negotiate data, privacy, and security terms (DPAs, security exhibits, cross-border transfers) within the Security team’s playbook, and bring in the AGC, Commercial or Privacy for anything outside it.

    Review AI vendor terms, such as training on our data, output ownership, and model changes.

    Build and scale vendor contracting operations.

    Build out and maintain our vendor playbook in Claude, so the whole team works from the same guidance and low-risk deals move without bottlenecks.

    Design and improve intake, triage, and approval workflows with FinOps.

    It has been revealed that own the vendor and procurement workflow in Ironclad, including intake, templates, approvals, and the repository, working with Legal Ops, who own the platform. Use it to track renewals and notice windows with FinOps and flag spend concentration risks.

    Create training and self-serve resources for business partners, and raise the visibility of the contracts function as a business enabler.

    Recent findings suggest that 6 to 8+ years of experience negotiating procurement, vendor, or technology transactions contracting, ideally buy-side at a U.S. SaaS or technology company, with deep knowledge of SaaS, cloud, and software licensing terms.

    A track record of negotiating directly with vendors and their counsel, independently and at pace.

    Strong working knowledge of privacy, data protection, and security terms in commercial contracts, including DPA negotiation and international data transfers.

    Experience designing contracting processes that are consistent, transparent, and easy for the business to follow.

    Clear writing and speaking, with the ability to explain legal and commercial risk plainly and the judgment to know when to hold a position, approve a reasonable risk, or escalate.

    Comfort using AI tools, Claude in particular, with sound judgment about when to rely on outputs, how to verify them, and how to protect confidential information.

    A degree in a relevant field (for example, law, economics, or political science), though we value experience over the specific degree.

    Sell-side experience negotiating customer, partner, or reseller agreements for a SaaS or technology company, which helps you see vendor terms from the other side.

    Hands-on experience with Ironclad or a similar CLM tool (Juro, Docusign CLM) or building AI-assisted legal workflows, ideally with some exposure to AI governance.

    Experience working across jurisdictions or with distributed, international teams.

    Experience at a fast-growing, developer-focused, cloud, security, or open source company.

    According to recent reports, supabase covers 100% of health insurance for employees and 80% for dependents, wherever you are. Your wellbeing and your family’s health are crucial to us.

    We operate asynchronously and trust you to manage your own time. You know what needs to be done and when.

    Every team member receives an annual education allowance to spend on learning—courses, books, conferences, or anything that supports your growth.

    #158511. Industry News: D+ Research: Brand’s holiday marketing tactics shift in 2026

    📅 23 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 5m • 📚 Deep Dive (924 w)
    📖 Baca
    General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Digiday ↗ Open Full Page

    Industry News: D+ Research: Brand’s holiday marketing tactics shift in 2026

    📅 23 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (924 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Digiday

    ⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • 1-3 in Nashville for the Digiday Programmatic Marketing Summit.
    • In a recent development, this research is based on unique data collected from our proprietary audience of publisher, agency, brand and tech insiders.
    • This is an excerpt from our Digiday+ Research report The 2026 guide to holiday marketing strategies, including A-Frame Brands, Mastercard and Ritual, which examined which commerce channels are dominating marketers’ holiday strategies.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Join us Dec. 1-3 in Nashville for the Digiday Programmatic Marketing Summit.

    In a recent development, this research is based on unique data collected from our proprietary audience of publisher, agency, brand and tech insiders. It’s available to Digiday+ members. More from the series →.

    This is an excerpt from our Digiday+ Research report The 2026 guide to holiday marketing strategies, including A-Frame Brands, Mastercard and Ritual, which examined which commerce channels are dominating marketers’ holiday strategies. The report is based on a survey of 90 brand and retailer professionals, as well as individual interviews with marketing executives.

    Digiday’s survey found that brands and retailers initiative to adjust the marketing tactics they’ll use during the 2026 holiday season in comparison to those they used in 2025.

    The biggest changes are that CTV/streaming and TV ads are gaining traction in 2026, with year-over-year increases of 22 percentage points and 20 percentage points, respectively.

    Recent findings suggest that forty-five percent of survey respondents said they plan to use CTV/streaming ads this holiday season, in comparison to 23% of respondents who said the same in 2025. The 2026 uptick followed a 14 percentage point dip in usage from 2024 to 2025.Meanwhile, marketers’ usage of TV ads remained relatively stable between 2024 and 2025, dropping by only 4 percentage points between 2024 and 2025, but grew by a whopping 20 percentage points in 2026. Thirty-three percent of brands and retailers said they plan to use TV ads this holiday season in comparison to 13% of marketers who said the same in 2025.

    Industry observers note that “Streaming is a really valid channel to invest in during holiday because consumption of that media spikes,” said Laura Brodie, chief growth officer at supplement manufacturer Ritual. “But participating in streaming is actually a decision for the whole year. Starting to engage just for holiday would be a risky move, especially for a smaller brand.”.

    “If you have the data to back it up over the course of the year showing this is a channel that’s proven and the ROI metrics associated, it can make a lot of sense to spike it during holiday,” she added.

    Recent findings suggest that ari Bloom, founder and CEO of brand incubator A-Frame Brands, noted that both streaming and TV ads can be effective for targeting specific demographic groups during the holidays. “Streaming and television is an effective audience conversion mechanism, especially with women over 30 years old,” Bloom said. “We’ve done a lot of work on daytime TV and on QVC. We see significantly bigger segments in the holiday time period from November through mid-December, and we always put attention on those times.”.

    It has been revealed that last year, brands’ and retailers’ most-used holiday marketing tactic was brand experiences, but that strategy fell to second place in 2026 behind streaming/CTV ads. Forty-one percent of marketers stated they expect to use brand experiences as a marketing strategy during the 2026 holiday season in comparison to 50% of marketers who said the same in 2025 — a drop of 9 percentage points.

    It has been revealed that brands and retailers are also divesting from using gift guides and influencer hauls/unboxing videos this holiday season. Marketers’ usage of gift guides decreased by 19 percentage points in 2026 vs. 2025, while their use of influencer hauls/unboxing videos fell by 14 percentage points this year in comparison to last year.

    Although gift guides and brand experiences decreased in marketer usage for the 2026 holidays, they remain brands’ and retailers’ top performing holiday marketing tactics over time. Thirty-one percent of marketers remarked gift guides have historically performed the best for their manufacturer during the holiday season, while 28% of marketers said the same of brand experiences, putting them in the No. 1 and No. 2 ranking spots, respectively.

    Although some marketers are shifting away from using gift guides for the upcoming holiday season, Ritual’s Brodie mentioned gift guides are likely to gain importance in the AI-driven search era because AI-powered search tools often rely on best of lists and curated recommendations to answer consumer queries.

    Industry observers note that “Gift guides are very interesting in the world of AEO and thinking about LLM optimization,” Brodie mentioned. “Overall, best of lists and gift guides are a close sister to [AI search results]. Gift guides can play an crucial role in holiday and especially bridging LLM research and AI overviews. So, I’m bullish about gift guides.”.

    Although brands and retailers are leaning into CTV/streaming ads for the 2026 holidays, those marketing tactics tied in the No. 4 spot for the best-performing holiday marketing tactic over time, while pop-up shops ranked No. 3. Influencer hauls/unboxing videos was the only marketing strategy that fell in both best historic performance and marketers’ intended use during the 2026 holiday season.

    A-Frame Brands’ Bloom said brands and retailers should also consider investing in catalogs for the 2026 holiday. “Catalogs have always been very successful, and they’re heavily conversion-focused,” Bloom explained. “When they’re discount-driven and when people’s attention is on buying, you can do offers that you can only get via physical paper, and it does drive people into stores.”.

    As social trends accelerate, brands like General Mills are scoring creator posts for shareability to bridge the gap between organic buzz and paid media.

    Dick’s is betting that youth sports can fuel its next phase of ad growth through GameChanger—if it can overcome limits on scale.

    As Black Friday Cyber Monday rapidly approaches, brands are most focused on acquiring upcoming customers this holiday season.

    #158506. Agencies are selling AI efficiency — clients want outcomes

    📅 23 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 4m • 📚 Deep Dive (861 w)
    📖 Baca
    AI & Tech ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Digiday ↗ Open Full Page

    Agencies are selling AI efficiency — clients want outcomes

    📅 23 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (861 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Digiday

    ⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Recent findings suggest that join us Dec.
    • Recent findings suggest that agencies spent the last two years pitching AI to clients as a cost story.
    • Clients do not hire agencies to be fast.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Recent findings suggest that join us Dec. 1-3 in Nashville for the Digiday Programmatic Marketing Summit.

    Amol Waishampayan, co-founder, fullthrottle.ai.

    Recent findings suggest that agencies spent the last two years pitching AI to clients as a cost story. Faster work, leaner teams, lower fees. Clients took the meeting, nodded along and then waited for the invoice to shrink. It didn’t. AI strategies now sound interchangeable to clients, who say the savings never demonstrated up in their fees.

    That is not an AI problem. It is a positioning problem. Efficiency was the wrong promise. Clients do not hire agencies to be fast. They hire them to grow the business. AI’s real opportunity for agencies is not doing the same work cheaper. It is doing work that actually moves revenue, and proving it.

    According to recent reports, agencies are getting operational value from AI. According to the Digiday Media Agency Report 2026, 70% of agencies say AI has cut costs by making tasks more efficient, while 31% say it cost more to implement than expected. But efficiency is a one-time gain.

    Once every agency has it, nobody gets paid for it. As one Gartner analyst told Digiday, the honeymoon between agencies and AI is “essentially over.” The agencies that build their AI story on productivity are competing on margin. The ones that build it on performance are competing on value, and value is what clients renew.

    Recent findings suggest that most media plans are still organized by channel. Search budget here, social budget there, streaming over in a separate deck. AI makes that structure obsolete, because it can blueprint around the customer instead.

    It has been revealed that take a regional home services tech giant running paid search and social. Those campaigns are producing something more valuable than clicks: a live stream of households actively researching its services. AI can turn those signals into a defined first-party audience, figure out where else those households spend their time, and extend the initiative into streaming TV, digital video and audio to reach them there. One audience, coordinated across channels, built from the client’s own demand rather than a platform’s inventory.

    Sources indicate that that is a different kind of planning. The question stops being “what should we spend on CTV” and becomes “who are we trying to reach, and where are they?”.

    The next step is letting AI act on that intelligence. Agentic systems can take audience and performance signals and adjust targeting, channel mix and spend as conditions change, instead of waiting for the monthly optimization meeting. Static plans with quarterly reviews are a relic of how long it used to take humans to read the data.

    Sources indicate that but here is where agencies should be careful. The advantage is not how much of the buying you automate. Anyone can automate. The advantage is whether the agent is optimizing toward something that matters. An agent chasing cheaper CPMs will find them, and the client will not care. An agent optimizing toward the client’s actual business outcomes, with the agency keeping full transparency and control, is a different product entirely.

    Sources indicate that this is the part most of the industry still avoids. Clicks and impressions are easy to report and nearly impossible to defend in a budget conversation. The only metrics a CFO cares about are sales, customers and revenue.

    According to recent reports, AI makes closing that gap practical. Bring together the advertiser’s first-party customer data, its transaction history and campaign exposure, and one can see which households were reached, which ones became customers and which channels and audiences did the work. Done with privacy-first, household-level methods rather than individual tracking, this is not surveillance. It is the client’s own data finally answering the client’s own question.

    It has been revealed that once that loop exists, everything upstream improves. Planning gets smarter because it is fed by real conversions. Agentic buying gets better because it is optimizing toward revenue instead of proxies. And the agency walks into every renewal with proof rather than a deck.

    Sources indicate that agencies are already monetizing AI. Digiday’s report found that 59% are launching new AI-powered products, 34% are selling strategic roadmaps or audits and 31% are charging additional fees for AI-powered services. But if the product is “we have AI,” the pricing power will not last. Every competitor has AI. Within a year, every client will have it too.

    The agencies that win the next cycle will not be the ones with the most AI. They will be the ones who can show a client exactly what it delivered, in the client’s own numbers. Efficiency gets agencies a thank-you. Outcomes get agencies the next three years of the account.Partner insights from fullthrottle.ai.

    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Industry observers note that kit is the email marketing platform experts choose to grow their audience, deepen their relationships, and build a business around the work they love. For coaches, YouTubers, authors, podcasters, and other creatives, there isn't a better marketing hub to rely on to grow audiences, automate email marketing, and sell digital products — all within one platform.More importantly, there isn't a team more committed to helping creators earn a living. We're on a mission to help creators earn $1 billion using our creator marketing platform. We have always been 100% independent and 100% remote.We are proud to have built a product that our customers love, and we look for people who have enthusiasm and belief in our mission, vision, and values to join our team. We're also embracing AI thoughtfully — both in how we build and how we hire to ensure our team is adaptable, innovative, and ready for what's next.

    According to recent reports, most Kit creators don't have a dedicated Creator Growth Manager, and when their emails start landing in spam, they need someone who can find the cause swiftly and explain it in plain language. We're looking for a Deliverability and Compliance Specialist to own deliverability support for that long tail of creators, run Kit's abuse desk, and make the compliance calls that protect the sending reputation every creator on Kit shares.

    Industry observers note that you'll also build the playbooks, training, and AI-assisted workflows that help Support and contractors handle more deliverability questions on their own, and you'll partner with our infrastructure engineers as we run more of our sending in-house. A creator can't build a lasting business if their emails don't arrive, so this work connects directly to our mission.

    It has been revealed that this is a full-time individual contributor role for someone who likes digging through headers and bounce logs to find the real cause of a problem, can explain DMARC alignment to a first-time creator without jargon, and is comfortable making a firm call when a situation is gray. You don't wait for someone to tell you what needs fixing. You proactively spot opportunities, identify patterns, and take the initiative to improve deliverability before problems arise.

    You'll report to Alyssa Dulin, Director of Creator Success, and collaborate closely with:.

    Our Deliverability team: a Deliverability Lead who supports our highest-value accounts and leads deliverability education, and a Deliverability Specialist who onboards and ramps up large senders moving to Kit.

    Our infrastructure engineers, who run Kit's sending infrastructure.

    Our compliance and anti-abuse engineers, who build the automated checks that keep spammers off Kit.

    Product Specialists and the Support team, who handle the front line and escalate deliverability problems to you.

    Customer Success Managers (we call them Creator Growth Managers at Kit), Sales and Migrations, and Product Managers.

    Sources indicate that first Week: Get set up in Kit, our admin tools, and our support and ticketing systems, and meet our distributed team in Get To Know You chats (GTKYs). Meet the deliverability team and get an introduction on the current projects. Read our deliverability playbooks and SOPs, and get access to the monitoring tools you'll use every day: Google Postmaster Tools, Microsoft SNDS, blocklist monitoring, and our internal delivery dashboards.

    First Month: Shadow the Deliverability team and Product Specialists on deliverability tickets, account approvals, and abuse reports, then start answering queue tickets with review. Join the daily monitoring rotation (blocklist delisting, Postmaster and delivery monitoring) and the weekly Deliverability team meeting. Learn how account approvals, compliance flags, and our in-house sending platform work. By the end of the month, work deliverability tickets and abuse reports on your own and send your first delisting requests. Project: build a recurring report showing the trending deliverability ticket reasons so we understand what’s causing how to reduce friction for customers and how to solve it.

    In a recent development, first Six Months: Own the deliverability support queue for creators without a dedicated CGM: spam-folder placement, bounces, authentication and DMARC setup, and escalations from Product Specialists. Own compliance end to end, from new-account approvals and compliance flags to pausing or closing accounts that put our shared reputation at risk.Run Kit's abuse desk. You'll write and share a strategy that covers coverage, response-time targets, escalation paths, and quality checks, then put it in place so routine spam, phishing, and blocklist reports follow clear SOPs while you take the hardest cases yourself. Be the go-to contact for day-to-day mailbox provider challenges with Microsoft, Gmail, Yahoo, Comcast, and regional providers, and write an incident runbook for blocklistings and provider throttling. Track the queue with a simple scorecard (volume, first response time, and escalation rate) and share what you learn with the team. Run training sessions for Support and ship your first process or AI improvements, like cleaner ticket categorization or better account data for our AI support agent, so more deliverability tickets get solved without escalation..

    First Year: Deliverability support is faster and more consistent for every creator on Kit, including the ones who never talk to a CGM. Your playbooks, help center articles, and AI-assisted workflows are what Support, CGMs, and contractors reach for first, and fewer tickets need to come to you. You've led at least one cross-team fix with infrastructure for a recurring problem you spotted in the queue, such as an alert when a creator's domain authentication breaks or a check for sudden signup spikes. You're helping shape the internal tooling and alerting our in-house sending needs, and you take part in industry groups like M3AAWG.

    Deep working knowledge of email authentication (SPF, DKIM, DMARC, alignment, and BIMI basics), plus the ability to read raw message headers and SMTP bounce and deferral codes.

    Hands-on use of Google Postmaster Tools and Microsoft SNDS/JMRP, and comfort working with major blocklists (Spamhaus, Abusix, Barracuda, Spamcop, and others) and their delisting processes.

    Data fluency: you can pull bounce, complaint, and engagement data together, find the root cause, and explain it so others can act on it.

    Hands-on abuse handling: you can work an abuse report or escalation start to finish, from finding the account and assessing the evidence to acting, replying to the reporter, and documenting the decision.

    Process building: you can turn repeat work into SOPs, playbooks, and quality checks that a contractor or teammate can follow.

    Clear, calm written communication with creators, teammates, and postmasters.

    Using AI tools to research, summarize, and draft, and helping teammates do the same, with the judgment to keep a person on final compliance calls.

    Experience with MTA logs or delivery observability tools (KumoMTA, PowerMTA, Postfix, Kibana/Elasticsearch, or SQL and BI tools like Mode).

    Familiarity with feedback loops, spam traps, list bombing, and bot-signup patterns.

    Familiarity with CAN-SPAM, CASL, and GDPR as they apply to marketing email.

    Experience with Intercom, HubSpot, or a similar ticketing tool.

    Experience building or tuning AI support workflows or macros.

    4+ years in email deliverability, compliance, trust and safety, or technical support at an ESP, mailbox provider, or high-volume sender.

    Handling escalated customer tickets end to end, including with customers who are frustrated.

    Making account-level compliance or abuse decisions, such as approving, suspending, or closing accounts.

    Working an abuse desk or abuse mailbox directly: spam and phishing complaints, provider and blocklist reports, and escalations.

    Leading the fix for a recurring deliverability or compliance problem that needed help from more than one team.

    Supporting senders on shared IP pools at an ESP.

    Setting abuse or trust and safety strategy, or directing contractors or vendors on a support or abuse queue.

    Working directly with mailbox provider postmaster teams.

    Participating in M3AAWG or other industry groups.

    Creating educational content, like help docs, training, workshops, or podcasts.

    Working with creators, digital entrepreneurs, or small businesses.

    You pick up problems that fall between teams without waiting for permission, and you follow them through until they're closed.

    You test a hypothesis against the evidence before you act, and you frame problems clearly enough that others trust your analysis.

    You protect the reputation every creator shares while staying fair and kind to the creator in front of you, and you help them understand the reasoning behind a decision.

    You turn what you learn into docs, templates, and training that others use, and you adjust how you teach to fit the audience.

    You hold a high bar for your work, and you push back respectfully, with data, when something puts our reputation at risk, even when Sales or leadership would prefer a different answer.

    You share in-progress work and risks early so the team can solve problems together.

    Treating deliverability as a set of macros rather than an investigation that needs judgment.

    Discomfort saying no to a creator or a teammate when our shared reputation is at stake.

    Waiting for someone to assign you work when you can already see the problem.

    Needing a fixed playbook, since our sending stack and processes are changing as we bring more sending in-house.

    Keeping knowledge in your head instead of writing it down for the next person.

    Preferring to work without AI tools.

We do our best to keep things reasonable, but a little time zone juggling comes with the territory.

    For this role, we're looking for someone based in North America, with working hours that give us solid US time zone coverage of the deliverability queue.

    The next test for agentic media

    📅 23 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (791 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Digiday

    ⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • 1-3 in Nashville for the Digiday Programmatic Marketing Summit.
    • Anudit Vikram, Chief Product Officer, Channel Factory.
    • Advertisers are building AI systems around the way their teams already work.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Join us Dec. 1-3 in Nashville for the Digiday Programmatic Marketing Summit.

    Anudit Vikram, Chief Product Officer, Channel Factory.

    Advertisers are building AI systems around the way their teams already work. These teams have their own agents, their own data and their own rules for what an agent may and may not do. At the same time, most of the specialized intelligence they depend on still sits inside separate vendor platforms.

    Industry observers note that as a result, vendor intelligence shapes a recommendation while remaining disconnected from the system acting on the recommendation. When planners carry conclusions between tools, the evidence and conditions behind those recommendations often fall away.

    Recent findings suggest that that’s the problem agentic media has to solve next. Can the intelligence behind the agent go where the work happens?

    It has been revealed that models and agent frameworks are widely available. Two vendors can build on the same foundation and ship agents that look identical in a demo. What separates them is what the agent knows, and whether the advertiser can put that knowledge to work. In media buying, that knowledge is specific.

    According to recent reports, A broad content classification offers only a starting point for a media decision. Suitability depends on the particular advertiser and market, and those judgments can change swiftly when breaking news alters the significance of a placement. A general-purpose model can’t reconstruct that brand-specific knowledge or historical context from a prompt alone. Classification depth and performance history can.

    Recent findings suggest that for Channel Factory, that means IAB 3.0 classification across more than 15 million YouTube channels, and more than 10 years and $4 billion of campaign performance data. To be clear, this isn’t an argument for keeping that intelligence locked inside a platform; it’s the opposite. Intelligence that only works inside its owner’s interface is as limited as a capable agent no one can reach.

    So the test is portability. Can an advertiser’s own agent call on a provider’s intelligence directly, from inside the planning and buying environment it already uses? That’s how Channel Factory is building, with contextual and suitability intelligence made available through APIs and MCP servers, and delivered through modular agents that run inside an advertiser’s environment or alongside it.

    With this architecture, market-specific suitability analysis becomes part of an advertiser’s own planning process. An agent can evaluate inventory against the provider’s classifications and historical performance data, applying the relevant standards for each market. Those findings can directly inform the plan, with the advertiser’s existing rules governing what the agent can recommend or change.

    Sources indicate that portable intelligence doesn’t mean identical agents. Two advertisers can draw on the same underlying intelligence and make different decisions. For instance, one avoids content when signals are unclear while another favors reaching inside defined boundaries. Both are valid because the thresholds, priorities and approval rules are the advertisers’.

    An agent’s knowledge source shouldn’t determine the scope of its authority. The brand decides what acceptable judgment looks like. The provider keeps the classification, history and models current.

    Learning needs the same discipline. Feedback and outcomes should refine recommendations, but advertisers should decide what shapes future decisions and which policies stay fixed. On its own, a successful campaign shouldn’t rewrite a brand’s suitability standards.

    Intelligence that moves into someone else’s systems has to carry its accountability along. As agents shift from recommending to acting, teams need to see what changed, why and whether it stayed within approved limits.

    Industry observers note that the principle is simple: Agents do the reasoning, and the engine owns the state, so every action is authorized, logged and traceable to the signals behind it. People define the strategy. Autonomy is earned in stages: alerts first, then recommendations, then bounded actions. An agent might make a small budget adjustment under set conditions while sending a larger change for human approval. How much authority to delegate is the advertiser’s call, and the system should make that call easy to enforce and easy to review.

    As agentic capabilities spread, feature lists will converge. Advertisers should look underneath the interface and put three questions to any provider:.

    The providers who can answer those clearly will matter more as brands take greater control of how they buy media. The rest will be unrealized demos.

    Accurate sales data gives our team a clear picture of the pipeline and the confidence to make informed decisions. That’s what makes this role so important.

    Your primary focus will be Sales: the dbt models that turn our CRM data into trusted pipeline, deal, and funnel metrics, and the Omni dashboards our sales leader and Senior Revenue Operations Manager use to run the business. You'll also model creator commerce data, so we understand what creators sell and earn through Kit, and you'll pick up reporting work with our Product team, such as feature usage reporting. On a small data team, we step outside our usual lanes when the need is there, so the mix will shift over time.

Teammates increasingly answer their own questions by querying our semantic layer through Omni's AI and MCP connections to AI tools. That means your models, metric definitions, and documentation need to be clear and correct enough for an AI agent to use them without a data teammate in the loop.

    According to recent reports, this is a full-time individual contributor role for someone who likes being close to the business, enjoys turning messy operational data into numbers people trust, and is happy to work on both the models and the dashboards that sit on top of them. When Sales and Product have clear, reliable data, we help more creators build more valuable businesses with Kit.

    You'll report to Sam Umachi, Head of Data (Linkedin).

    It has been revealed that within our data team, you'll work alongside a Staff Analytics Engineer who owns org-wide semantic layer governance and modeling standards, a Senior Data Engineer who owns ingestion and pipelines, and a Senior Business Analytics Partner focused on revenue opportunities. This role has no direct reports.

    Recent findings suggest that first Week: Work through our onboarding curriculum in Notion and meet the data team, our Senior Revenue Operations Manager, the sales team, and your product partners. Get set up in our core tools: dbt Cloud, GitHub, Amazon Redshift, Omni, HubSpot, Linear, Hightouch and Slack. Set up your AI-assisted development environment and learn the shared AI workflows our data team uses. Open and merge your first small pull request so you learn our review and deployment flow early.

    First Month: Map how HubSpot objects (deals, pipelines and stages, companies, contacts, and owners) flow into our dbt models, and document the gaps. Take over day-to-day ownership of the sales models and Omni dashboards that teammates have been covering. Audit current sales reporting and list where definitions differ or numbers don't reconcile. Share a written reflection with the team on what you've learned and where you'd focus first.

Leave your domains well documented and well tested, legible to fresh teammates, stakeholders, and the AI agents that query our semantic layer.
