    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    According to recent reports, join us Dec. 1-3 in Nashville for the Digiday Programmatic Marketing Summit.

    Amazon is paying OpenAI to reach the same shoppers it refuses to let ChatGPT study.

    After a relatively quiet few months on the chatbot following its Prime Day activity, the e-commerce giant has returned to the platform with a upcoming round of Black Friday ads in the U.S., Digiday has seen.

    In a recent development, the ads, which are the same format as typical ChatGPT ads — separate from the user conversation, with a favicon, headline, description and a “Learn more” call to action — are appearing in ChatGPT in the lead-up to Black Friday. They promote Amazon Black Friday deals and direct customers to Amazon to complete their purchases.

    In a recent development, what’s different compared to other retailers, though, is how ChatGPT is surfacing Amazon products and deals. Rather than directing users to individual product pages, ChatGPT’s shopping experience is linking to Amazon search results, while drawing on third-party deal-tracking websites to identify products, discounts and up-to-date pricing. That means ChatGPT can help consumers discover Amazon products and compare deals without necessarily accessing Amazon’s own website directly.

    It has been revealed that amazon’s increased activity on ChatGPT is interesting given the retailer already operates its own shopping ecosystem and one of the world’s largest ad businesses. Its presence on the chatbot puts it in the position of using a competing platform to drive shoppers back to its own marketplace, while that same platform is developing its own way of facilitating product discovery around Amazon’s catalogue.

    Amazon also has an opportunity to monetize that traffic once shoppers arrive on its marketplace.

    “Sending shoppers to Amazon search results rather than individual product pages also creates another opportunity to make money from advertising,” remarked Arielle Feger, senior analyst, commerce media and retail at eMarketer.

    It has been revealed that amazon’s U.S. search ad revenues are forecasted to reach $40.57 billion this year, nearly a quarter of all U.S. search ad spending. Traffic coming from ChatGPT gives Amazon another opportunity to put sponsored products in front of shoppers.

    Industry observers note that “For brands, that creates a risk of paying twice for the same customer,” Feger added. “Even after winning a recommendation in ChatGPT, a brand could find itself paying again to compete against sponsored listings on Amazon.”.

    But Amazon’s relationship with ChatGPT extends beyond buying ad space for its own products.

    In September, Amazon Ads unveiled a partnership with OpenAI that allows advertisers to buy ChatGPT inventory through Amazon’s DSP, extending their existing Amazon ad campaigns onto the chatbot. The integration initially gives select U.S. advertisers access to ChatGPT’s ad inventory through Amazon DSP, giving brands another route to reach consumers using the AI chatbot.

    What is unclear is whether Amazon has bought its ChatGPT ads directly from OpenAI, or through its own DSP.

    Both Amazon and OpenAI declined to comment on this article.

    Tech Report: Ad Tech Briefing: Meta eyes CTV as AppLovin circles Criteo, signs of the squeeze on independent ad tech

    📅 24 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1203 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Digiday

    ⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Industry observers note that join us Dec.
    • This Ad Tech Briefing covers the latest in ad tech and platforms for Digiday+ members and is distributed over email every Tuesday at 10 a.m.
    • AppLovin’s reported interest in Criteo and Meta’s prepares to explore CTV could put further pressure on independent ad tech, with some companies reporting challenging circumstances in the latest round of earnings calls.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Industry observers note that join us Dec. 1-3 in Nashville for the Digiday Programmatic Marketing Summit.

    This Ad Tech Briefing covers the latest in ad tech and platforms for Digiday+ members and is distributed over email every Tuesday at 10 a.m. ET. More from the series →.

    AppLovin’s reported interest in Criteo and Meta’s prepares to explore CTV could put further pressure on independent ad tech, with some companies reporting challenging circumstances in the latest round of earnings calls.

    Last week, Reuters reported unconfirmed acquisition discussions involving AppLovin and Criteo, the same day Next in Media reported that Meta was exploring partnerships with television manufacturers and free FAST services to extend its advertising platform into CTV.

    If both sets of developments materialize, it would represent two of the largest established (mobile) ad platforms expanding into new channels using existing advertiser relationships, data, and buying technology.

    It’s well understood that AppLovin wants to extend its performance advertising business beyond mobile applications, and Criteo — a company that is reportedly seeking an exit from the public markets — could provide retail relationships, commerce data, and access to advertisers across the open web.

    Meanwhile, Meta could use its existing buying platform to help advertisers reach television audiences without relying on a separate demand-side platform.

    In recent weeks, separate sources told Digiday this could prove a key advantage in helping the social networking outfit eat into Google’s lead in markets where its DSP, DV 360, dominates.

    However, developments could reduce advertisers’ dependence on independent DSPs and supply-side platforms.

    AppLovin’s potential shortcut into commerce.

    Private equity firms Vista Equity Partners and Quinti Capital have also reportedly expressed interest in Criteo, which has engaged an investment bank to evaluate its options.

    AppLovin reported third-quarter revenue of $2.19 billion, up 55% year over year, alongside $1.44 billion in net income.

    Criteo reported a 12% revenue decline to $416 million, with net income falling to approximately $6 million.

    AppLovin’s growth has been driven by mobile advertising, although the company is increasingly targeting e-commerce advertisers outside of gaming.

    Criteo has spent years expanding beyond retargeting into commerce media, developing relationships with retailers, access to shopper data and cross-channel advertising capabilities.

    Per official figures, Criteo’s commerce intelligence draws on more than $1 trillion in annual transactions, 740 million daily active users and over 5 billion product SKUs, and acquiring it could accelerate AppLovin’s expansion into retail media, providing relationships and data it would otherwise need to develop independently.

    However, integrating the businesses would be complicated given that AppLovin’s core technology is built around mobile apps, while Criteo operates across retailers, publishers, and other commerce environments.

    The potential benefits would depend on whether their different data assets, buying systems, and commercial relationships could work effectively when integrated.

    Earlier in the year, multiple sources told Digiday that Meta is ⁠exploring an option that would allow advertisers to extend campaigns into third-party television inventory through its existing advertising tools — a measurement tactic commonly known as audience extension.

    The latest reporting suggests Meta is considering how those relationships could support an advertiser-facing buying option, resembling Pinterest’s CTV audience-extension offering, which lets advertisers use Pinterest’s audience data to reach consumers beyond its owned properties. Meta could pursue a similar approach at considerably greater scale.

    Its existing advertiser base could access television inventory without establishing separate relationships with specialist CTV buying platforms, an attractive option for smaller advertisers already using Meta’s automated campaign tools.

    For DSPs and SSPs, the competitive implications would be significant, as Meta could bring more advertisers directly into CTV, potentially reducing the role of intermediaries that connect buyers with television inventory.

    In a recent development, but questions remain about how the proposed model would operate. For example, would Meta determine which inventory advertisers purchase? Plus, how would fees and media costs be disclosed? And what independent measurement would be available?

    Such details are likely to determine whether Meta’s proposed offering creates a meaningful alternative to existing CTV buying arrangements or simply adds another layer between advertisers and publishers.

    AppLovin’s interest in Criteo and Meta’s reported CTV expansion reflect a broader shift in advertising technology, as larger companies with bigger advertiser bases and proprietary data extend their buying capabilities into additional channels. Amazon is pursuing a similar strategy through its DSP and retail media business, which is morphing into a unified agentic platform.

    The Trade Desk’s recent financial performance illustrates the difficulties facing some independent players. The firm reported a 0.5% third-quarter revenue decline to $736 million, marking a rare contraction after years of sustained growth, and is on course to simplify and offer fresh measurement capabilities as it attempts to restore growth.

    While The Trade Desk’s recent revenue decline cannot be attributed to Meta’s reported plans or AppLovin’s potential acquisition, the contrast provides context for broader competitive pressure on independent buying platforms.

    The emergence of unified media platforms is another response, as ⁠last week’s explainer outlined; these systems aim to coordinate advertising across search, social, programmatic, and direct publisher relationships.

    But coordinating buying across platforms is not the same as controlling the underlying inventory, data, or optimization technology. Independent companies will need to demonstrate value beyond simplifying workflows, particularly as AI makes campaign execution easier.

    For independent ad tech, maintaining a meaningful role in that environment will become increasingly difficult.

    According to recent reports, figures from ⁠HUMAN Security’s BADBOX 3.0 investigation, published Nov. 18.

    ⁠WTF is a unified media platform?

    The industry’s emerging buying platforms promise to coordinate advertising across channels, but their ability to control actual spending decisions remains contested.

    ⁠Ad Tech Briefing: Google’s antitrust troubles aren’t over.

    Google’s European antitrust exposure and The Trade Desk’s financial difficulties illustrate the challenges facing established ad tech businesses.

    “Global Privacy Control (GPC) WebKit API, for all you browser and browsing experience developers out there.”.

    — John Wilander, Apple’s privacy frontman, introduces a software revision that will let app developers let users signal their preference to opt out of data sharing and cross-context targeted advertising, a right supported by regulations like the CCPA.

    ⁠Anthropic says no to ads, but Wall Street may have other ideas.

    Anthropic’s opposition to advertising raises questions about whether the company can maintain that position as the cost of developing and operating AI models increases.

    ⁠Ampersand is offloading its indie agency business to Comcast and Spectrum following mass layoffs.

    Ampersand’s restructuring and the transfer of its independent agency business to Comcast and Spectrum highlight the pressures facing traditional television advertising intermediaries.

    ⁠AI-driven tech layoffs suck, but might lead to certification.

    Jonathan Bellack examines how AI coding tools are reducing opportunities for junior engineers, and considers whether professional certification could help establish fresh standards for software development.

    ⁠Tech companies are trying to shift the entire concept of privacy again.

    The Electronic Frontier Foundation examines how technology companies are attempting to redefine privacy protections as AI systems create newly introduced opportunities to collect and process personal information.

    FutureSight’s newly introduced tool can help banks of all sizes get a side-by-side idea of how their media mix stacks up against the competition.

    HUMAN Security’s latest investigation queries the effectiveness of CTV verification safeguards.

    Walmart is letting Meta’s Muse shop its shelves — but on its own terms

    📅 24 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (783 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Digiday

    ⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • 1-3 in Nashville for the Digiday Programmatic Marketing Summit.
    • By letting Meta’s Muse agent into its stores only through the gateway it built and controls, Walmart is treating AI agent access the way retail media networks once treated ad slots: as inventory to be doled out on its own terms.
    • The retailer is preparing to launch a connector to Muse that will provide the AI agent with defined access to its e-commerce infrastructure, meaning it gets to set the guardrails and boundaries within which Meta’s agent can browse and shop.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Join us Dec. 1-3 in Nashville for the Digiday Programmatic Marketing Summit.

    By letting Meta’s Muse agent into its stores only through the gateway it built and controls, Walmart is treating AI agent access the way retail media networks once treated ad slots: as inventory to be doled out on its own terms.

    The retailer is preparing to launch a connector to Muse that will provide the AI agent with defined access to its e-commerce infrastructure, meaning it gets to set the guardrails and boundaries within which Meta’s agent can browse and shop.

    The capability was noticed by Juozas Kaziukėnas, founder of e-commerce research firm Marketplace Pulse, after he spotted an patch to Walmart’s technical instruction manual for Muse. According to The Verge, that integration launches tomorrow (Nov. 24), in time for Black Friday Cyber Monday shopping.

    The manual, which Digiday has also seen and verified, describes how Muse can interact with Walmart’s shopping systems on behalf of a user. This includes tasks like searching for products, answering questions, building shopping carts and, if permission is granted, completing orders. Muse can also call on Walmart’s own shopping assistant Sparky to answer questions about products, stores and comparisons.

    So a Walmart Shopper could ask Muse to compare three televisions, find specific ingredients for a dinner party, or ask the agent to add products to its Walmart shopping cart. Muse can then use Walmart’s systems to carry out those tasks. For example, Walmart could help Muse identify a customer’s usual brand of milk without handing over their entire shopping history.

    This goes beyond what someone might typically expect from a chatbot, where a user might simply ask for recommendations. Instead, Muse, through the gateway to Walmart’s own marketplace, can act on those recommendations, taking care of the legwork involved in shopping and even making purchases once the user has given the necessary permission.

    Walmart talked about its vision for this in its blog post last month.

    Sources indicate that built using the Model Context Protocol (MCP), the integration gives AI agents a more direct and reliable way to interact with Walmart’s shopping systems. It’s designed to let agents shop on a customer’s behalf without giving them access to their wider purchase history or unnecessary personal information. For example, Walmart could help Muse identify a customer’s usual brand of milk without handing over their entire shopping history.

    Industry observers note that walmart has also started introducing Agent Profiles, which gives each AI agent its own dedicated profile within a customer’s Walmart account. It means shoppers can distinguish purchases made by an AI agent from the ones they’ve completed themselves, while deciding how much autonomy they want to give the agent. Customers can require approval for every purchase, or set a spending limit (such as $50, $100 or $200), allowing the agent to spend up to that amount without seeking approval each time. Customers also have the ability to disable the agent’s access at any time.

    In a recent development, this development comes after Amazon already blocked Muse from accessing its e-commerce site in September, arguing that third-party AI agents should operate openly and respect retailers’ decisions about whether to participate. At the time, Amazon stated it asked Meta to remove its website from Muse’s shopping experience, but Meta declined. It also raised concerns about Muse accessing customer accounts without authorization and potentially capturing customer credentials. However, Meta disputed the claims, saying Muse cannot see users’ passwords or payment details.

    Industry observers note that while Walmart might be working closer with Muse going forward, this approach could raise questions about its ad business. In particular, with Muse increasingly allowed to take over product discovery, where does that leave its sponsored product placements and how much influence will brands have over what an AI agent recommends.

    It has been revealed that “There will emerge a upcoming advertising mechanism where brands will pay dollars not for a sponsored placement, but for a ‘sponsored consideration’ to the agents,” said Abhishek Bora, head of digital growth at All Star Elite. “If agents take over the buying process, how would a new brand with a better product and offer get considered by an agent when it has no history of reviews, usage or purchases?”.

    Neither Walmart nor Meta responded to Digiday’s request for comment.

    As social trends accelerate, brands like General Mills are scoring creator posts for shareability to bridge the gap between organic buzz and paid media.

    Dick’s is betting that youth sports can fuel its next phase of ad growth through GameChanger—if it can overcome limits on scale.

    As Black Friday Cyber Monday rapidly approaches, brands are most focused on acquiring new customers this holiday season.

    #158480. Why brands are writing no-AI clauses into creator deals

    📅 24 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 3m • 📚 Deep Dive (680 w)
    📖 Baca
    AI & Tech ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Digiday ↗ Open Full Page

    Why brands are writing no-AI clauses into creator deals

    📅 24 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (680 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Digiday

    ⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • 1-3 in Nashville for the Digiday Programmatic Marketing Summit.
    • In a recent development, influencer marketing contracts have become a focal point in the creator economy.
    • “We actually are seeing more and more contracts including language around the creator not being able to use AI in their content for these campaigns,” remarked Kurt Stadelman, vp of talent at creator marketing firm Pearpop, in a conversation with Digiday managing editor Sara Jerde during Digiday’s recent Creator Strategies event.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Join us Dec. 1-3 in Nashville for the Digiday Programmatic Marketing Summit.

    In a recent development, influencer marketing contracts have become a focal point in the creator economy. There’s heightened attention being paid by brands, creators and creators’ representatives to deal terms, such as usage rights, exclusivity and payment terms. But among the newest addendums is AI usage.

    “We actually are seeing more and more contracts including language around the creator not being able to use AI in their content for these campaigns,” remarked Kurt Stadelman, vp of talent at creator marketing firm Pearpop, in a conversation with Digiday managing editor Sara Jerde during Digiday’s recent Creator Strategies event.

    Sources indicate that creators are actually welcoming brands’ no-AI demands, he stated. Creators are already concerned about generative AI being used to create content and crowd out creators from people’s feeds. So brands forbidding AI-generated content from creators signals a commitment by brands to human-made content, said Stadelman.

    According to recent reports, but what counts as AI-generated content? Does it prohibit the creator from using AI tools in any part of their process?

    “We’ve had to specify that a few times just to make sure, because obviously you want the creator to be able to use AI tools in the background when they’re developing their concept or their script. Even utilizing AI to analyze their past performance of their content and advise them on their strategy moving forward. And I think brands should probably embrace that because it ultimately helps the creator deliver the best version of themselves and the best content possible,” remarked Stadelman.

    Here are a few highlights from the conversation, which have been edited for length and clarity.

    It’s way too risky to be only utilizing organic posting for creator campaigns and just hoping that the right people see it. We are seeing more and more brands utilize paid behind whether it’s white-listing or utilizing the creator content as an ad unit for themselves on their own channels. Along with that comes, obviously, you have to write the paid usage rights into the contract, and most brands are good about that.

    The wrong length for usage rights.

    Usage in perpetuity should never be agreed to. That’s a dangerous place to be for a creator and can negatively impact their future collaborations with other brands in the same category. Exclusivity, obviously, is quite difficult for a lot of creators if they agree to a longer exclusivity term than they should. That limits their options moving forward.

    The right length for usage rights.

    Sometimes you’ll see proposed terms that are just a little too lengthy with the usage rights. We push back on that sometimes. I don’t think there’s any reason to be agreeing upfront to any more than six months of paid usage. Even that’s a bit lengthy. Starting it at three months if they’re really wanting to utilize paid with the campaign, that makes sense. Even up to six months is fine in most cases. But once you get to that point six months from now, you can reassess and extend if you’d like. But I don’t think there’s any reason to go beyond that in the initial contract.

    Recent findings suggest that we always push for shorter payment terms. If somebody’s asking for net-90, we try to push for net-60 or, ideally, net-30. But I understand that some brands have their standard operating procedures there, which is fine. But we just ask that they honor those payment terms, which is a whole other problem that we’re seeing happen more and more, is that brands are just not honoring these payment terms that they’ve themselves written into the contract.

    📅 25 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 4m • 📚 Deep Dive (782 w)
    📖 Baca
    General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Digiday ↗ Open Full Page

    Banking gets a helping hand in media modeling from SpendSight

    📅 25 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (782 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Digiday

    ⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • It has been revealed that join us Dec.
    • It’s easy to know what your bank balance is, in the age of apps and online banking.
    • Mediastruction, an independent media agency that two years ago debuted FutureSight, a SaaS platform dedicated to speeding up media mix modeling, is drilling into specific industries.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    It has been revealed that join us Dec. 1-3 in Nashville for the Digiday Programmatic Marketing Summit.

    It’s easy to know what your bank balance is, in the age of apps and online banking. It’s not as easy for banks to know how effective their marketing efforts are.

    Mediastruction, an independent media agency that two years ago debuted FutureSight, a SaaS platform dedicated to speeding up media mix modeling, is drilling into specific industries.

    Sources indicate that the brainchild of Marilois Snowman, who founded Mediastruction and FutureSight, SpendSight puts a specific lens onto the banking industry. It’s a free benchmarking tool that enables bank marketers to evaluate their media budgets to see if their spending aligns with their peers.

    Recent findings suggest that snowman said conversations with clients and with other banks that aren’t yet clients told her there’s an information gap in the sector. “It’s a problem for mid market in general,” she explained in reference to other subscription media tools. “Sometimes mid-market brands don’t show up at all, or then they’re just wildly inaccurate.”.

    For small banks, this information is pretty important, agreed Mark Gibson, marketing practice leader at Capital Performance Group. “It’s not uncommon in the banking industry to have one or two people in the marketing department, and maybe not even an ad or media agency,” he stated. “Media is like you know 1/20th of your job, so by definition, you’re not going to be very sophisticated about about what media is available and how you should allocate it. For that kind of advertiser, this kind of stuff can be really valuable.”.

    Industry observers note that snowman also noted that some media, from search to social and CTV, aren’t even properly tracked by other services. “Given the percentage of investment that is digital media these days — I mean, what isn’t digital media? — it just seems to be a substantial gap.”.

    According to recent reports, mediastruction built SpendSight from a proprietary 2026 survey of financial institution marketers, and Snowman said it’s the first of its kind to capture how banks and credit unions actually split paid media dollars across channels. To date, about 100 different banks and credit unions have participated in the survey, giving them access to the findings.

    Any bank marketer enters their budget and channel mix, which lets SpendSight generate a side-by-side comparison against the peer average, flagging where they’re over- or under-invested. All inputs and responses to the survey remain anonymous and the underlying survey data is never exposed.

    “All of that kind of discussion is really helpful for marketing teams to bring to executive leadership, and then to be able to sell through shifts in media looks and modeling engagements,” remarked Snowman.

    So what has SpendSight determined? Initial results show some patterns with how banks and financial services have been marketing, and which media channels they’re relying on. Although it comes as no surprise that digital performance channels make up about 51% of the average media mix, broadcast and traditional media (linear TV, radio, print, out-of-home) still account for roughly 38%. (Interestingly, the American Bankers Association’s Banking Journal cited more than 60% digital spend, which Snowman attributed to differing channel definitions.).

    Within digital, paid search and paid social represent more than one-fourth of average spend (13.7% and 13.0%, respectively). Paid search is the most widely used channel, with 96% of institutions investing in it. As for other media, direct mail makes up 7.4% of the average mix and is used by 82% of institutions, which is more than linear TV, display, and online video (as anyone knows who gets mail at home).

    Gibson at Capital Performance Group, which participates in multiple surveys for banking including SpendSight, noted the reason he thinks SpendSight goes one step farther. “While [other studies] provide some useful benchmarking in terms of how much banks spend overall, and what various media are used, they don’t quantify the spend by media mix or by media channel,” he stated. “That’s the new innovation that this tool does.”.

    Sources indicate that it also gives Mediastruction lead generation to build up its potential client base with financial firms, which Snowman acknowledged. “What we really want to sell through is FutureSight’s modeling. We can use this as a free tool to get to know us to offer something of benefit to potential clients, that’s what our goal is.”.

    📅 25 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 3m • 📚 Deep Dive (689 w)

    Breaking: In Graphic Detail: How shoppers are adopting AI for product research ahead of Black Friday

    📅 25 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (689 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Digiday

    ⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • In a recent development, join us Dec.
    • Sources indicate that marketers are shifting ad dollars toward performance channels as the important Black Friday/Cyber Monday trading period approaches.
    • The places they find information about brands, the sources that information is based on, and what they do with that information are all changing.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    In a recent development, join us Dec. 1-3 in Nashville for the Digiday Programmatic Marketing Summit.

    Sources indicate that marketers are shifting ad dollars toward performance channels as the important Black Friday/Cyber Monday trading period approaches. Yet the way consumers use search — a crucial channel within performance marketing — is evolving rapidly, as they adopt generative AI tools like Gemini and ChatGPT to aid their purchasing decisions.

    The places they find information about brands, the sources that information is based on, and what they do with that information are all changing. Meanwhile, audience adoption of AI research is far from uniform across generations and markets, further complicating the picture.

    “Black Friday used to be won in the final week with the deepest discount and the loudest media,” stated Jonathan Verrall, vp of SEO at Jellyfish. “Now AI writes the shortlist weeks earlier from the sources shoppers trust. Advertisers who treat Black Friday as pure promo media are already late. The winners will initiative earned, owned and paid together from October and give AI data it can believe.”.

    In a recent development, what is certain is that the way brands seek to influence consumers during product discovery and research is shifting. With the year’s biggest sales event around the corner, read on for a data snapshot of the state of product discovery.

    According to a survey of 2,800 shoppers in the U.S. and U.K. conducted by Brainlabs in 2025 and 2026, the percentage of consumers using AI for product research rose on average from 6% last year to 13%. Clearly, more shoppers are using AI tools to compare and research the products they’re considering. While search engines themselves still led consumer practices, sources like Amazon and YouTube slipped.

    A Jellyfish study of citation sources, using U.K. Black Friday-related prompts the week beginning Nov. 16, found third-party sources leading the pack. That means blogs, news articles and comparison sites counted for more than brands’ own websites or retail listings in influencing AI chatbot representations of a brand or a product.

    This is borne out by other studies. In an analysis run for an unnamed client, PMG found a brand’s website supplied just 24 out of 203 links cited in AI answers recommending the client’s products. Only 22 went directly to its homepage.

    Even if they only account for a minority of citations, brands’ own sites, platforms and retailer listings are areas that an advertiser can control. Zooming in, not all retail platforms are equal, either. Amazon, Costco and Etsy’s sites have lost share of citations in recent quarters, while Target and Walmart have gained in recent months, according to data from Tinuiti and Profound.

    The hope that they might influence shoppers using AI tools for product discovery has been one of the motivations driving marketing dollars toward ChatGPT. Ad spend has risen month-on-month, according to estimates by AdClarity, which estimated total spend on the platform to have reached $116.6 million in October, with U.S. brands accounting for 64%. (The above chart is in millions of dollars.).

    Concerns with measurability and evidence that ChatGPT ads lead to greater conversions, however, may hold brands back from accelerating that spend as much as OpenAI execs would like.

    According to Bain, two-thirds of consumers use AI tools for general research, while 42% specifically use them to research products. But there are variations across generations.

    The McKinsey Agentic Commerce Consumer Survey, June 2026, surveyed 5,800 shoppers who’s used AI chatbots or search tools for a shopping task in the last three months. It found middle-aged and younger consumers are embracing the tech while older shoppers (who still hold plenty of disposable income) aren’t. It’s an vital distinction for brands targeting consumers in specific stages of their lives.

    As social trends accelerate, brands like General Mills are scoring creator posts for shareability to bridge the gap between organic buzz and paid media.

    Dick’s is betting that youth sports can fuel its next phase of ad growth through GameChanger—if it can overcome limits on scale.

    As Black Friday Cyber Monday rapidly approaches, brands are most focused on acquiring latest customers this holiday season.

    It has been revealed that curious about the kind of challenges you'll work on at Camunda? Watch this quick 30-minute talk from our engineers to learn more about the fresh Camunda Exporter and how we’re solving complex problems at scale.

    We are looking for a Product Builder to join the IDP & RPA pod. You will take real problems from customers, decide what is worth solving, and build and ship the solution yourself, using AI tools to get from idea to production quickly without lowering the bar.

    In a recent development, product Building is how Camunda's Experience organization builds the applications people use on top of Camunda 8, such as Hub, Operate, and ProcessOS. Small pods of builders own a product area from customer problem to shipped change, with no hand-offs between product management, design, and engineering. We are setting this model up now, so you will help shape how it works.

    Recent findings suggest that the IDP & RPA pod builds how Camunda processes work with documents and legacy applications. With intelligent document processing (IDP), customers create extraction and classification templates in Camunda Hub and publish them so a process can use AI to turn invoices and other documents into structured data. With robotic process automation (RPA), customers integrate legacy applications that have no APIs, using Robot Framework scripts on a standalone RPA worker. The hard problems come with putting LLMs into customer processes: extraction quality, model and prompt choices, testing and trust, and working for AI agents as well as for people.

    Help shape product direction for IDP & RPA by combining customer input, usage data, and field feedback into clear priorities.

    Partner with the other builders and product strategy to turn problems into shipped features, using short written proposals and prototypes to align early.

    Talk to customers and to support and customer success colleagues about how IDP is used and where it breaks, and turn what you learn into decisions about what to build next.

    Pick up customer incidents and trace them across Hub, the connectors, and the deployed process of the customer.

    Track what you ship against real outcomes and adjust when the data tells you to.

    #158464. The clipping economy is changing as platforms crack down and creators seek control

    📅 25 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 7m • 📚 Deep Dive (1315 w)
    📖 Baca
    General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Digiday ↗ Open Full Page

    The clipping economy is changing as platforms crack down and creators seek control

    📅 25 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1315 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Digiday

    ⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • According to recent reports, join us Dec.
    • Depending on who you ask in the creator economy, they might say that clipping is dead.
    • Industry observers note that the practice of sharing short clips from long-form content to boost the original content’s audience or promote a brand, exploded in popularity over the last few years, with major creators like Jimmy “MrBeast” Donaldson, Cody “Clix” Conrod, and Eric “Airrack” Decker starting their own clipping companies.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    According to recent reports, join us Dec. 1-3 in Nashville for the Digiday Programmatic Marketing Summit.

    Depending on who you ask in the creator economy, they might say that clipping is dead.

    Industry observers note that the practice of sharing short clips from long-form content to boost the original content’s audience or promote a brand, exploded in popularity over the last few years, with major creators like Jimmy “MrBeast” Donaldson, Cody “Clix” Conrod, and Eric “Airrack” Decker starting their own clipping companies. It catapulted certain creators into the spotlight and encouraged brands to hire clippers to give their branded partnerships extra airtime.

    In short, what began as fans sharing clips has grown into a billion-dollar distribution business.

    Sources indicate that but some platforms are now tightening the rules around clipping. TikTok and YouTube have been cracking down on non-original and mass reposting content. Last week, Instagram added a content protection feature previously available only on Facebook, which lets eligible creators automatically identify videos matching their original content. They can now see how those videos perform and decide whether to hide them from people on the platform, add a credit link, or let the videos stay up. That gives creators more visibility and control over where their content appears, making clipping less of an open-ended reporting play and more subject to the original creator’s say.

    “Creators deserve credit for the work they make,” a Meta spokesperson told Digiday. “[This] builds on our broader efforts to prioritize and reward original content and creativity over re-uploaded posts that don’t add a unique perspective or meaningful edits.”.

    And yet, platforms aren’t all moving in the same direction: Twitch is investing further into clipping to try and claw back the short-form real estate it’s ceded to other platforms. To understand what’s driving these diverging approaches, and what they mean in practice, Digiday spoke with seven experts across the clipping ecosystem.

    Industry observers note that “Ask 10 people [what clipping is] and you’ll probably get eight different answers,” stated Darren Clover, CEO of creator-led holding organization Full Box Inc., which owns Reach Clipping. “We define clipping as skilled editors taking existing source material and transforming it into unique pieces of short-form content…Those videos are then distributed across individual social accounts. That’s very different from downloading someone else’s TikTok and reposting the exact same video across hundreds of accounts.”.

    According to recent reports, opinions also differ around whether clipping works as a performance marketing channel or if it’s just a good distribution method. A few days ago, Brian Blum, host of the Only Sweat Equity podcast, posted on X that clipping “has actually always been dead.” He told Digiday he meant that it has never worked as a performance marketing channel.

    Sources indicate that blum’s concern is that clipping can produce impressive view counts without reaching people likely to buy. He said campaigns can be vulnerable to fraud and attract audiences that may not be a fit for the product.

    “It doesn’t have necessary protections to prevent viewbotting or fraud…So you’re actually just lighting money on fire,” he said.

    Nikolai Amirzadeh, co-founded of clipping firm Clip Tech, said clips can function as both marketing and distribution tools if the clipping company in question does the work to ensure views are valid.

    “It is priced like performance, you pay per 1,000 verified views and nothing for clips that flop. It behaves like earned media, because it is native posts from real accounts, not ads. Brands typically pay $1 to $4 per thousand verified views, against $10 to $80 or more for traditional paid social,” Amirzadeh stated. “Anything that looks off goes to the fraud team, and the clipper is not paid until it is cleared. A view is still a view by each platform’s own definition, which is a low bar. That is why the serious brands look at the top clips, watch time and what happens downstream, not just the view total.”.

    Then there’s the question of control: As clipping spreads and platforms tighten their rules, creators and their partners are increasingly concerned about how clips are edited and shared, and whether they could create brand-safety risks.

    According to recent reports, “Clipping is kind of a double-edged sword. It can help creators gain visibility and show that people value their content, but it could also get them flagged as spam,” remarked Ashray Urs, head of Streamlabs.

    Recent findings suggest that that lack of control gives creators and their managers pause, according to Reed Duchscher, CEO of Night Management. “It’s hard to control any of it,” he mentioned. “Even when you put out a bounty for someone to clip something, you still have very limited control of what is posted, how it’s posted,” he added, pointing to the common practice of people clipping streamers out of context to farm outrage or drama.

    Instead, their clients, like mega creator Kai Cenat, have their own in-house clippers, which allows for more control and, crucially, legitimate measurement.

    Industry observers note that expect this to be an increasingly popular approach in the next year. “Sometimes with these clipping companies you can’t understand if the views are legitimate or not…you don’t know if they’re paid views or not paid views because you’re not controlling the TikTok accounts and not posting the videos. So we’re a little nervous about that,” Duchscher said.

    With platforms cracking down on recycled content, the age of the clip farm may be over. But clipping itself isn’t.

    Mustafa Aijaz, vp of media tech giant SoaR, thinks clipping is no longer a low-effort gold rush. “A quick cut and post won’t get you very far,” he said. “You need a different caption, some commentary, or a breakdown — something that adds to the raw clip itself. If you’re different, the platform treats you differently. But if you look exactly like the other posts, you’ll likely be throttled.”.

    And as the demand for clips has grown, some have leaned into the more negative aspects of clipping, like taking creators out of context or clipping moments that are less than flattering. This influx of negative framing or drama farming has shifted creators’ opinions on external clippers.

    Add that to the clipping companies’ increased selectiveness and rising rates, and something’s gotta give, according to Brandy Merriweather, founder and senior PR executive at BSTarPR.

    “Many successful clipping pages have secured partnerships with gambling entities, music labels, creator management companies, creator collectives, and streaming platforms. Consequently, they are becoming more selective about which creators they post, their rates, and the frequency of posting for specific creators,” she mentioned.

    Merriweather told Digiday she’s seen creators have to pay extra money to clippers to switch priority streaming platforms.

    Industry observers note that “It’s a SUBSTANTIAL business filled with egos, narrative control, fabricated numbers, unethical and sometimes purposely false content all going to the highest bidder,” she stated. To avoid price gouging or unfair depictions, creators need to take clipping into their own hands. “What used to be a vehicle to gain visibility has now turned into an accountability stage that creators have no control over since many don’t own these pages. The creators, their families, and their teams are being used to create drama and fuel negativity which algorithms have prioritized because of the engagement….It’s a system many helped build that now controls them.”.

    Merriweather’s solution matches the other experts Digiday spoke with: creators have to create their own clipping networks to ensure they have control over their content and a proper understanding of how it’s performing.

    Cody “Clix” Conrod is a professional Fortnite player with over 26 million followers and nine creator-focused businesses. Now he has his own holdco.

    Breaking: Digiday+ Research: A-Frame Brands, Ritual and other brands prioritize new customer acquisition this holiday season

    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • 1-3 in Nashville for the Digiday Programmatic Marketing Summit.
    • Industry observers note that this research is based on unique data collected from our proprietary audience of publisher, agency, brand and tech insiders.
    • As Black Friday and Cyber Monday rapidly approaches, brands are most focused on acquiring upcoming customers this holiday season.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Join us Dec. 1-3 in Nashville for the Digiday Programmatic Marketing Summit.

    Industry observers note that this research is based on unique data collected from our proprietary audience of publisher, agency, brand and tech insiders. It’s available to Digiday+ members. More from the series →.

    As Black Friday and Cyber Monday rapidly approaches, brands are most focused on acquiring upcoming customers this holiday season. They’re also eager to turn those seasonal shoppers into repeat buyers.

    It has been revealed that fifty-nine percent of brand and retailer professionals stated that upcoming customers are the primary audience for their 2026 holiday advertising. That’s down just one percentage point from the 60% of marketers who said the same last year, indicating that customer targeting trends have not shifted significantly.

    Less than half of survey respondents (41%) remarked that existing customers are the main audience for their holiday marketing, up one percentage point from 40% in 2025.

    The holiday season’s influx of shoppers gives brands an annual opportunity to attract latest customers and to build lasting relationships beyond the initial purchase.

    According to recent reports, ari Bloom, founder and CEO of brand incubator A-Frame Brands, estimates that brands see a 20% to 30% increase in latest customers as a percentage of total during the holiday season, as consumers look to discover products and brands. “It is a time period where you can acquire a lot of new customers… when we naturally see new customers come into the holiday funnel,” Bloom noted.

    He also expects AI to play a central role in 2026 holiday marketing, changing how consumers find and buy products. “AI is probably going to become one of the most important funnels for new customers because, instead of using old habits to discover existing brands, there’s a whole other ‘person’ shopping for them,” Bloom mentioned. “Just as we see people relying more on AI agents, you’re going to see more new brand exploration and customer acquisition from the brand side.”But acquiring new customers is only part of the equation. Brands also need to give existing customers a reason to return.

    Laura Brodie, chief growth officer at supplement firm Ritual, said brands can encourage repeat purchases by offering exclusive perks, seasonal products and other incentives. “Being able to pull people back who have shopped before by creating a compelling gift with purchase, seasonal drop or something similar is one way,” Brodie said. “If you don’t have the budget to support units, having something that feels intentional for an existing customer base is another.”.

    In a recent development, brands with similar consumer bases should also consider partnering on gift-with-purchase offers, according to Brodie. “The cost of acquisition is high during the holidays, so being able to tap an existing audience can be really cost-effective,” she mentioned. “Similar-sized brands can create something that feels compelling [to consumers] and benefits both brands — potentially an offer swap. We’ve had success partnering with brands like Osea on a swap gift with purchases.”.

    As social trends accelerate, brands like General Mills are scoring creator posts for shareability to bridge the gap between organic buzz and paid media.

    Dick’s is betting that youth sports can fuel its next phase of ad growth through GameChanger—if it can overcome limits on scale.

    Product discovery habits are changing, leaving marketers unsure how to pivot ahead of the biggest sales period of the year.

    #158458. In Graphic Detail: The GTA 6 creator industrial complex

    📅 26 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 6m • 📚 Deep Dive (1279 w)
    📖 Baca
    General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Digiday ↗ Open Full Page

    In Graphic Detail: The GTA 6 creator industrial complex

    📅 26 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1279 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Digiday

    ⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • In a recent development, join us Dec.
    • Recent findings suggest that the most anticipated modern video game, Grand Theft Auto 6 (GTA 6), was released a week ago today, selling $3.79 billion in just a single day of sales.
    • According to analytics website Stream Charts, GTA 6 beat every other major game’s full-week watch time in just two days, and did so with ease, hitting 214.6 million hours watched in two days, versus the next highest game, Valorant’s 150.48 million hours in a week.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    In a recent development, join us Dec. 1-3 in Nashville for the Digiday Programmatic Marketing Summit.

    Recent findings suggest that the most anticipated modern video game, Grand Theft Auto 6 (GTA 6), was released a week ago today, selling $3.79 billion in just a single day of sales. Creators have been preparing for GTA 6’s release for years, figuring out ways to stand out from the millions playing the game and the thousands of people making content around it.

    According to analytics website Stream Charts, GTA 6 beat every other major game’s full-week watch time in just two days, and did so with ease, hitting 214.6 million hours watched in two days, versus the next highest game, Valorant’s 150.48 million hours in a week.

    According to recent reports, “A record was never in doubt. Rockstar’s gameplay reveal in August already drew close to 4 million concurrent viewers, for a game nobody could play yet,” Streams Charts product manager Nazar Babenko told Digiday.

    In a recent development, A week later, let’s take a look at how the GTA 6 creator economy over the last week (and the months leading up to it), including the livestream watch hours, the most popular platforms, the top streamers, and the organic cultural conversation around the game. Just how big is GTA 6? Unsurprisingly: Huge.

    Industry observers note that ahead of GTA 6’s launch, platforms saw a marked increase in content around the franchise and the previous game, GTA 5, which introduced in 2013. Streamlabs reports that GTA 5’s year-to-date viewership was higher than several other major, more current video games.

    Streams Chart’s seven-day GTA 6 numbers showcase the game generated more watch time on Twitch alone than any previous game launch had across all platforms the company tracks.

    “Hours watched surprised us more than the peak,” stated Babenko.

    Creators who built a name and audience for themselves making GTA 5 content have been preparing for GTA 6 for over a year (the game release, initially slated for November 2025, was delayed twice, and the game was officially announced in 2023).

    It has been revealed that reed Duchscher, CEO and founder of talent agency Night Media, said that GTA creator Andre “Typical Gamer” Rebelo (who has 16.3 million followers on YouTube), has perfected his video-on-demand content (VOD) with GTA 5 and was prepared for GTA 6. “He’ll have a bunch of video concepts that he’ll go film away from his livestream and then post on YouTube because most people will be so concerned about beating the campaign,” Duchscher said. “He has a wealth of knowledge from GTA 5 and a huge catalog on YouTube, so we know what video concepts are going to do well.”.

    According to recent reports, according to Streams Charts, there were over 125 million hours watched of GTA 6 gameplay in just 24 hours (November 18 to November 19). Twitch drove the most views, accounting for 1.7% of views (market intelligence firm Sensor Tower reports Twitch mobile app downloads and daily active customers increased by more than 80% day over day on those two days), then YouTube, which pulled in 35.1%. Kick came in third with 22.1%, while other live streaming platforms made up the difference – which was still over 1.3 million hours of watch time.

    It has been revealed that notably, YouTube organized a 24-hour livestream with some of its top creators, but was still beaten by Twitch, possibly because the platform unveiled during TwitchCon 2026 that it would be giving away copies of the game through surprise daily drops. Both Twitch and YouTube added custom GTA 6 badges, animations, and effects.

    Though Twitch edged out YouTube for livestream watch hours in the first day of GTA 6’s launch, YouTube still saw over 3.5 billion global views of videos with GTA 6 in the title the day of release. To date, YouTube reports the Grand Theft Auto series has over 900 billion views, and that GTA 6 videos hit 40 billion views before November 18.

    It has been revealed that within the first week since launch, there have been 420 million hours watched of GTA 6 across all major platforms, with peak viewers hitting 7.91 million. Stream Charts reports the game has been mentioned in livestream chats over 3.2 million times across more than 55,000 channels, with sentiment almost split between positive and negative – that could be largely attributed to the online reactionary response to some gameplay elements that involve fixing up a nice and being nice to your girlfriend.

    Recent findings suggest that unsurprisingly, perhaps the biggest streamer in the world, Darren Jason “IShowSpeed” Watkins Jr., drew the most eyes during the first 24 hours post-release, with 4.7 million watch hours across YouTube and Twitch. Close behind him was a streamer known as The Burnt Peanut, with 3.8 million watch hours across YouTube, Twitch and Kick.

    In third was Brazilian streamer Alan “Alanzoka” Ferreira, who notably generated 3.1 million hours watched during launch day solely on Twitch.

    In just a week, GTA 6 has edged out some of the most popular streaming categories and video games, drawing more views than Kick’s entire IRL stream category, and drawing close to its Just Chatting category. As of halfway through 2026, Just Chatting had become the most-watched category across all major streaming platforms, signaling that they were shifting from gaming-focused content to more IRL and commentary content. But GTA 6 appears to have shifted the livestream platforms back to what they were first made for: Gaming.

    A broad “gaming” category is the most-watched on all of YouTube within the last month, and the fourth-most watched on Twitch. Even GTA 5, the previous installment in the franchise, ranked in the top ten most-watched categories over the last 30 days. Gaming is back, and creators will likely lean further into its popularity, especially those who don’t typical game.

    According to Streams Charts, 1,056 channels reached a new all-time peak viewership record while streaming GTA 6, with the most records held by YouTube creators. According to the week after launch report, almost one in five record-breaking channels received at least ten times as many concurrent viewers as their pre-GTA 6 peak.

    According to data pulled by influencer marketing agency Linqia, the GTA 6 hype was almost entirely organic. Its creator data pulled during the pre-launch GTA 6 period (April 1 through November 18), shows that 97.8 percent of creators posting about GTA 6 were doing so organically, with just 2.2 percent sponsored. Rockstar Games did not pay a single creator who took part in Linqia’s study, while 7 percent of the paid creators came from prediction market Kalshi – notably not a gaming brand.

    “The most active brands were the platforms,” remarked Babenko. Two-thirds of creators talking about GTA 6 never even mentioned a brand. According to Linqia, it seems sponsorships might actually hurt content performance: sponsored posts that name-dropped GTA 6 performed 3 percent worse than each creator’s typical sponsored post. You can’t fake the GTA 6 hype.

    “I think a lot of brands leaned in from an organic social standpoint but many outside of gaming didn’t think creator first for GTA,” noted Keith Bendes, chief strategy officer at Liniqia. “Which was a significant missed opportunity since creators were clearly talking organically about the game in droves.”.

    Cody “Clix” Conrod is a professional Fortnite player with over 26 million followers and nine creator-focused businesses. Now he has his own holdco.

    The creator economy is shifting its stance on clipping as platforms crackdown; what does clipping look like in the future?

    💡 Key Takeaways
    • 1-3 in Nashville for the Digiday Programmatic Marketing Summit.
    • Dick’s Sporting Goods has found that there’s significant business in youth sports.
    • The sporting retailer recorded a third quarter GAAP net income of $161 million in earnings this week — more than double the $75 million reported the year prior.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Sources indicate that join us Dec. 1-3 in Nashville for the Digiday Programmatic Marketing Summit.

    Dick’s Sporting Goods has found that there’s significant business in youth sports.

    The sporting retailer recorded a third quarter GAAP net income of $161 million in earnings this week — more than double the $75 million reported the year prior.

    Dick’s execs attributed much of that success to Dick’s Media Network, home to its youth sports app GameChange.

    Like many long-tail retail media networks, Dick’s Sporting Goods doesn’t break out its ad business revenue by dollar figure or percentage. Dick’s chief financial officer Navdeep Gupta noted that the company is grappling with supply-chain related costs, higher fuel costs and other pressures, but Dick’s Media Network partially offset those pressures.

    Industry observers note that “We have talked about these gross margin growth drivers with Dick’s Media Network and GameChanger. Those are continuing to be very differentiated drivers of not only our profitability, but our gross margin expansion,” he mentioned.

    It has been revealed that dick’s Media Network is four years old and offers ad units in-store, on its own site, off-site across the open web, social and streaming. Perhaps its biggest get is its live sports via GameChanger.

    “They found this gap in the marketplace in terms of sports club video streaming. And they’ve created this app, this solution, and now they inherently have their own O&O [owned and operated] inventory from a media perspective,” stated Olivia Hawkins, vp of media strategy at Salt XC.

    Dick’s has previously worked with sports brands like Adidas, On, Under Armor and Crocs. However, the sports retailer is actively engaging non-endemic partners too.

    Sources indicate that take Chobani, for example. The yogurt brand bought ad space on Dick’s Sporting Goods Game Changer app during the 2026 FIFA World Cup, remarked Hawkins, who was familiar with the deal.

    In a recent development, she did not disclose financial details of the ad buy. The campaign focused on reach and awareness, getting Chobani in front of youth sports enthusiasts, like parents and coaches, Hawkins mentioned.

    “They met our expectations in terms of reaching a new audience and delivery, frequency, and all those media metrics — CPM and video completions and all that,” she said, without detailing the campaign’s success.

    Dick’s video app CPMs are more premium, hovering around $35, according to one commerce executive who spoke on the condition of anonymity.

    “That’s more expensive than big TV. They’re asking for that price for that type of inventory. It’s a great solution — super clever, but it’s expensive,” the anonymous exec told Digiday. In comparison, Netflix CPMs fell from their initial $60 when it introduced in 2022 to the low $20s right now.

    Seemingly, brands are willing to cough up the dough. That’s the bet Dick’s seems to be making. It makes sense given sports has become the industry’s latest golden goose.

    Sources indicate that put some numbers on it. In a survey this year, Dick’s Media and eMarketer reported that 63% of U.S. parents have kids in youth sports and 84% of them stated youth sports influence their buying choices.

    Now, there’s the question of scale. Dick’s GameChanger app has more than 5 million monthly active people, but youth sports is more niche than something like the National Football League, which averages 18.7 million viewers per game during the regular season.

    It has been revealed that “It’s a great audience. It’s a great inventory, but it is finite versus other offsite environments that include all of the open web,” Hawkins mentioned.

    That leaves Dick’s in the same boat as other retail media networks — or at least every other RMN that isn’t Amazon or Walmart — where continued growth may have to come from beyond retailers’ owned and operated channels.

    As social trends accelerate, brands like General Mills are scoring creator posts for shareability to bridge the gap between organic buzz and paid media.

    As Black Friday Cyber Monday rapidly approaches, brands are most focused on acquiring new customers this holiday season.

    Product discovery habits are changing, leaving marketers unsure how to pivot ahead of the biggest sales period of the year.

    Support the wider team: help write security advisories for our customers, answer customer security questions and support audits.

    General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Digiday ↗ Open Full Page

    Brands race to systematize how to know what makes creator content worth paying for

    📅 26 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (903 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Digiday

    ⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Industry observers note that join us Dec.
    • According to recent reports, social media trends move faster than brands can keep up with.
    • Sources indicate that take General Mills, for example.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Industry observers note that join us Dec. 1-3 in Nashville for the Digiday Programmatic Marketing Summit.

    According to recent reports, social media trends move faster than brands can keep up with. Now, they’re trying to create repeatable systems to turn organic social attention into something they can evaluate, fund and ultimately scale.

    Sources indicate that take General Mills, for example. Home to brands like Cheerios, Cinnamon Toast Crunch and Trix, the CPG brand has spent the past year putting together an internal framework to systematize monetizing viral moments.

    Its “talkability score” is a calculation used to measure whether General Mills’ brands are earning more attention with social media creators than they’re buying with paid ads. It’s a loose framework that varies by brand, Mindy Murray, director of influencer and content at General Mills mentioned, and generates a score based on whether users shared it, put their own spin on it and how long interest in the trend lasts.

    Murray was mum on the actual mechanics on how it actually determines whether to invest ad spend. “We’re weighing on earning, we’re weighing things like active engagement — so shares likes, comments, saves — because we know that that means someone took an actual effort to do something versus just an impression,” Murray said.

    Virality can’t be manufactured, but this “operating system” allows them to “go faster and be smarter,” remarked Murray.

    Over the past year, General Mills has also reorganized its teams to bring social and influencer marketing under Murray’s purview, she told Digiday, to move more rapidly and efficiently in converting buzzy organic content into paid ads.

    For example, over the summer Reese’s “Eat ‘Em Up” cereal jingle from the early 2000s started trending on TikTok. General Mills noticed the trend, partnered with GloRilla to re-record the rap, tracked real-time activity via its framework, and ultimately turned it into a campaign on streaming platforms and Reese’s Puffs’ YouTube channel. The company boasted a 2.5% year-over-year sales increase as a result, but did not provide specific sales figures. The company did not say specifically how the framework informed that strategy.

    Last week, influencer agency Billion Dollar Boy (BDB) rolled out its Creator Investment Planner, a financial modeling tool that aims to help marketers understand the ad spend levels required to plan and “de-risk creator investments,” according to a news release.

    Recent findings suggest that BDB’s tool works by calculating blended CPMs from creators and social media platforms. Marketers enter their budget and time frame, and the platform calculates estimates for share of voice, total impressions and earned media value. Per BDB, the model can update as inputs change, where marketers can expect to “de-risk” spend commitments.

    Industry observers note that and in April, CreatorIQ creator platform and creative analytics and governance platform CreativeX released a upcoming tool to help brands incorporate creator content into a paid media strategy. The system works on an API, sending creator content from CreatorIQ’s platform to CreativeX to be graded, reviewed by CreativeX’s AI-powered system and optimized by a brand campaign manager. Ultimately, it aims to identify creator posts with potential to do well as an ad before any media buyers open their wallets. Nestlé was the first brand to sign on. The integration was revealed on an invite-only basis.

    To agency execs, all signs point to brands getting more rigorous about their spend — especially when it comes to squeezing performance out of creators — and do it before the trend disappears.

    Recent findings suggest that creator spend is expected to increase 12% every year until 2030, according to advertising research firm Madison & Wall. In no small part, brand spend on boosting or promoting creator content is fueling that growth.

    “Before any sort of budget is unlocked, you have to be able to prove out that there’s a higher propensity for that piece of content for whatever investment you’re making into social to actually move towards a conversion,” said Madison Gaudry-Routledge, evp of social at Viral Nation, a social agency.

    Most brands, Gaudry-Routledge remarked, haven’t come up with a named framework in the same way General Mills has. Brand spend on creator marketing is expected to grow twice as fast as spending on advertising. Naturally, brands are eager to see proof of concept as early as possible.

    Viral Nation has its own proprietary framework offered to clients as an add-on service. It’s called Culture Quotient that blends brand awareness, brand affinity and brand velocity into a measurable score to determine a brand’s relevance in cultural conversation. The tool works via AI that analyzes conversations and content, identifies emerging cultural trends and tracks shifts in consumer sentiment, per Gaudry-Routledge. The social exec declined to share any client-specific examples.

    These calculations are being built in real time and haven’t yet replaced traditional metrics like share of voice, audience sentiment and engagement.

    “As an industry, we’re continuing to try to catch up on operationalizing frameworks and systematizing measurement and still not there yet,” said Kristina Coughlin, svp and general manager of Trevant, a creator marketing agency.

    Dick’s is betting that youth sports can fuel its next phase of ad growth through GameChanger—if it can overcome limits on scale.

    As Black Friday Cyber Monday rapidly approaches, brands are most focused on acquiring latest customers this holiday season.

    Product discovery habits are changing, leaving marketers unsure how to pivot ahead of the biggest sales period of the year.

    This is a full-time individual contributor role ideal for someone who has added an upmarket sales-led motion to a product-led company before and wants their work measured in win rate and deal size.

Audit the sales content reps use today and how product usage at the moment routes accounts to sales. Set baselines with RevOps for win rate, sales cycle, deal size, and expansion revenue. Share a written point of view with the entire growth team on who our established creator buyer is and the three biggest gaps in how we sell to them.     Latest Update: The gaming creator with more than 26 million followers just launched his own holding company

    💡 Key Takeaways
    • In a recent development, join us Dec.
    • Industry observers note that this article is part of an ongoing series examining successful creator business strategies.
    • Cody “Clix” Conrod is a professional Fortnite player who regularly wins esports tournaments, and is also a wildly popular creator.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    In a recent development, join us Dec. 1-3 in Nashville for the Digiday Programmatic Marketing Summit.

    Industry observers note that this article is part of an ongoing series examining successful creator business strategies. More from the series →.

    Cody “Clix” Conrod is a professional Fortnite player who regularly wins esports tournaments, and is also a wildly popular creator. Conrod started playing video games at five years old, and began live streaming at 13. Conrod has amassed some 26 million followers across social media since (8.73 million followers on Twitch, over 5 million on YouTube, 6.7 million on TikTok, 2.86 million on X, 2.81 million on Instagram, and 848,000 on Snapchat).

    He’s the most-watched professional Fortnite player in the world, according to his team, but in the last few years, he’s been looking to grow beyond just esports content and branded partnerships with a portfolio of his own companies.

    Sources indicate that while still with talent agency Vayner Sports, Conrod was paired with agent Darren Glover, who said he was influenced by the career movements made by creators like Jimmy “MrBeast” Donaldson and the Dude Perfect team (who were forming their own entities and corporations). Glover wanted to apply this same approach to Conrod’s career — prioritizing fewer, more quality partnerships.

    In a recent development, “I tried to actually do half and half. I tried to be a halftime Fortnite professional and then a halftime content creator that also wants to work with brands. And I became not good at the game,” Conrod said, which pushed him to retain Glover.

    Glover was named CEO of Full Box Inc., the Conrod-led holding company that rolled out in early October, with Conrod as chief creative officer. Heading into this fall, Conrod was running his entire creator business through Clix Gaming, his creator-focused gaming media company. Full Box Inc. combines Conrod’s nine creator-focused companies and organizes them under three pillars: operating companies (Clix Gaming, Clix Creative, and Dr3amin Clothing), Full Box Ventures (Reach Clipping, Real Sports App, water filtration company Rorra, TapCaps PC collectibles, and lifestyle brand XSET), and Impact (Dr3amin Access Fund).

    “The change was not starting something latest, it was adding an umbrella over [the] top of everything,” stated Glover.

    Conrod may be following in the footsteps of other massive creators with millions of followers, but his positioning as a professional gamer first, content creator second, means his approach has to consider both professions. Sometimes, Conrod can’t stream his Fortnite gameplay during tournaments, as creators playing online games can often be “stream sniped,” which is when viewers watch a broadcast while also playing the same game and use the stream to find and kill the streamer in-game. This can cause players who are stream-sniped to lose tournaments. Glover helped Conrod scale his content to a point that, if he does go to a Fortnite tournament and isn’t streaming, he has a backlog of things to post that doesn’t require him to work late into the night to produce something post-tournament.

    Sources indicate that the holdco is the biggest step of many Conrod has taken to ensure his career can extend far beyond professional gaming. It’s one many video game creators may take in the future as they seek to generate revenue that isn’t tied to game updates or platform algorithms — or even their own face. Consider it the MrBeast business model.

    “I realized when I was 18, I wanted to build stuff larger than just me, where it could scale without my face all the time or me having to be there,” said Conrod.

    Conrod and Glover don’t just want to create products and agencies and sign brand deals, but extend into the philanthropy side of the creator space to cement his legacy.

    Industry observers note that conrod launched the Dr3amin Access Fund, which provides kids with the access and hardware needed to become professional gamers or gaming streamers. Last year, the fund delivered more than $250,000 in gaming equipment.

    Industry observers note that for now, partnerships still make up around half of Conrod’s revenue, with the balance split between ad revenue on Twitch, YouTube, owned royalties, and Fortnite’s unique Support-A-Creator program, which lets players back creators in Fortnite by giving them 5 percent of purchases made with their unique creator code. They did not share revenue specifics.

    According to recent reports, “Our business is profitable and runs without one single brand dollar,” mentioned Glover. “So brand dollars for us are investment vehicles of partnerships for us to do more, but we’re not putting ourselves at risk of being profitable or scaling our manufacturer based on other people’s dollars.”.

    He wants more creators to understand that they have some control over their revenue on platforms like YouTube and Twitch, or, in Conrod’s case, Fortnite, and that they can expand beyond just a basic sponsorship setup.

    “I want content people to feel like they are a major factor for the health of the business,” Glover added, “and I think we’ve been showing that we’re doing that, and we’re doing it really well.”.
